# Coding standards

- Minimal code. No speculative abstractions. No options nobody asked for.
- Prefer editing an existing file to adding one.
- Delete what is unused. No dead branches.
- Every exported function, component and type carries a one-line summary in the language's own doc format (JSDoc in TypeScript), then `@param` and `@returns` only when they say something the signature does not. Comments are single line and only where the code cannot say it. No comment blocks. No commented-out code.
- Every change is verifiable. If you cannot test it, say so before shipping it.
- Every value that crosses a boundary (HTTP response, WebSocket event, form data, storage, URL params, LLM output) is parsed into a typed shape (a Zod schema, or the generated contract types) right after it is read. Field access happens on the parsed value. Never `any` or `Record<string, unknown>` for a known shape.
- Treat LLM output as untrusted data: check the type before you call a method on it.
- A type that another repo reads or writes, or could later, lives in the shared contract package first (if this project has one), then is imported or generated here. Never define it here now and move it later. When in doubt it is shared; say so in the plan before writing it.
- Secrets never appear in code, logs, tests, or chat. `.env` files and key material are off limits; a hook enforces this. Anything prefixed for the client bundle is public by definition; never put a secret there.
- TypeScript `strict` is on. No `any`, no `as unknown as`, no `@ts-ignore`. Named exports. Function components with hooks; no classes. `bun run check` (format, lint, types) is the gate.
- Match the surrounding code's style, not its gaps. New and changed code is fully typed even when older files are not.
=================== .claude/agents/reviewer.md
---
name: reviewer
description: Adversarial reviewer for a branch or PR. Use before a human reads the diff. Finds correctness bugs, scope creep, missing tests and rule violations, then writes up the assumptions the author made.
model: opus
memory: project
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
---
You review code written by another agent or a person. You have not seen their conversation, so you do not share their blind spots. Be specific and be fair.

Input: a branch name or a PR number. Start with `git diff origin/main...<branch>` or `gh pr diff <n>`.

Cover all of:
1. Correctness. Does each hunk do what the commit message says? Trace inputs to outputs for anything that crosses a boundary. Read the receiving side's types.
2. Scope. Anything in the diff the task did not ask for? Name it.
3. Tests. New behaviour without a test, or a test that cannot fail.
4. Rules. Read `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/` and check the diff against them: strict TypeScript with no `any` or `as unknown as`, a Zod schema or generated type at every boundary, hooks declared before any early return, shared state through the store and never local state other components read, generated files untouched, JSDoc on every export, no dead code, no secrets in the client bundle.
5. Simplicity. Code that could be shorter or could reuse something that exists.

Output, in this order: findings ranked by severity, each with file, line and a one-line failure scenario; then the assumptions and design decisions you believe the author made, and why. One or two sentences per item; leave out anything that would not change what the author does next. Plain English.

Update your memory with recurring patterns you find in this repo, so the next review starts ahead. One pattern per entry with a one-line summary. Skip what CLAUDE.md and the rules already say, and fix entries that turn out to be wrong.

# Verify before saying done

1. Gates. Run what CI runs, from the frontend root: `bun run check && bun run test && bun run build`. Report the exact counts. A failure is reported as a failure, with the output.
2. Read back. Read `git diff` for every file you changed. Check each hunk does what the task asked and nothing more.
3. Side effects. For every function, component, type or constant you changed or removed, grep the repo for other users. Fix or list them.
4. Secrets. Scan the diff for keys, tokens, passwords, URLs with credentials. None may be in it. Anything prefixed for the client bundle is public.
5. Contract check, when the change reads data across a boundary (HTTP, WebSocket, storage, URL params, a generated contract): read the sending side's type definition first, not the docs, and parse explicitly.
6. Full-flow trace, when the change spans the live path and the history or reload path: name each hop and confirm the shape matches at each one. Run the component through the state transition that hits any early return.
7. Plan adherence, when working from a written plan: diff your output against the plan's fields, props and names. Anything missing or extra is a bug until the human says otherwise.

Then report: what was verified, what was not, and why.

I've read TASK.md and the whole skeleton repo, including every hook script, since those will run on my tool calls. Here's my summary for your review.

## 1. What TASK.md asks for

**The product:** a full-stack To Do app with a web client and our own backend API. You log in and then do full CRUD on your own tasks only.

| Area | Requirement | Hard or hint |
|---|---|---|
| Backend | A simple API. Storage can be in-memory, a file or a real database. Deploying it is optional. | Hard |
| Backend | REST style: resource URLs, standard HTTP methods, JSON. Status codes: **200/201 success, 400 validation error, 401/403 auth, 404 missing**. | Hint |
| Frontend | Talks to our API, has login, does CRUD on the user's own tasks, and is **responsive** | Hard |
| UX | Sign-in landing page, task list, **reorder**, **search**, a **detail screen** to view and edit a task | Hint (we'll treat all as in scope) |
| README | How to run it on a **Mac**. Bonus: deploying to distributed cloud infra. Also: approach, features done, what we'd add with more time and how long, how we'd make it more robust. | Hard |
| Code | In a shareable git repo and runnable. Community-standard style. **No debug logging, TODOs or FIXMEs**. Has test coverage. | Hard |
| Graded on | Clean, concise but descriptive code. Sound fundamentals. Tests. | Hard |
| Bonus | **TDD**. **Functional, declarative style** (higher-order functions, composition, map/filter/reduce, correct data structures). **Async through high-level abstractions**. | Bonus |

**The bar:** missing the minimum criteria ends the interview. So the hard deliverables, especially "we can run it", come before any bonus work. The live deep-dive also means every design choice needs a reason I can defend.

**Things that are easy to miss:**
- **FastAPI returns 422 for validation errors by default.** The hint asks for 400, so we need a custom handler.
- **"Has no debug logging"** rules out `print` and `console.log` in shipped code. I'd add a CI gate for that, not just a rule.
- **Test frameworks:** the task names Jest, Mocha, Chai and Enzyme. The skeleton uses Vitest, whose API matches Jest's, plus React Testing Library. Enzyme doesn't support React 18 or later. We'd explain this in the README; pytest covers the backend.
- **TDD only shows in git history.** Committing the failing test before the code that passes it is the evidence a grader can see.

## 2. What the skeleton is

`claude-ag` isn't app code. It's two Claude Code setup kits (`backend-python/` and `frontend-typescript/`), each with settings, 6 hooks, rules, 2 agents, 4 skills, and template `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` files.
- **Backend defaults:** FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy with alembic, pytest, ruff, uv.
- **Frontend defaults:** Vite, React, Bun, Vitest, Oxlint and Oxfmt, Tailwind, Zod.

**Safety:** the hooks use only the Python standard library and make no network calls. They only block commands or report lint findings.

**Tools:** git, gh (logged in as `arun98aol`), uv, Python 3.13, Bun 1.3, Node 24, pnpm and Docker are all installed.

## 3. Proposed skeleton setup

1. **Monorepo:** `backend/` and `frontend/` under one repo, since the task asks for "a git repository". It gets one root `.claude/` that merges both kits.
   - The Python, TS and React rules apply only to their own folder.
   - `map.json` paths get the folder as a prefix.
   - Each folder keeps its own `CLAUDE.md`.
2. **Fill every `{{TOKEN}}`.** Delete what doesn't apply: multi-env Appendix B, the tool-registry and WebSocket parts of the frontend docs, CONTRIBUTING §15–16.
3. **Add rules drawn from TASK.md:**
   - Functional, declarative style.
   - TDD with a visible red-then-green history.
   - No debug logging, TODOs or FIXMEs. Enforced by a CI grep gate and the `/verify` skill.
   - The HTTP status-code contract, including the 422→400 fix.
   - Ownership checks: another user's task returns 404, not 403, so the API doesn't leak which IDs exist.
   - Coverage thresholds in CI.
   - Responsive UI. Async through FastAPI and asyncio on the backend and TanStack Query on the frontend.
4. **CI:** GitHub Actions jobs for backend (ruff, pytest with coverage), frontend (check, test, build) and the hygiene gate.
5. **Git bootstrap:** the hook blocks commits on `main`, and a new repo needs a first commit there. I'd make one empty root commit on `main` before the hooks are copied in. All skeleton work then goes on `chore/repo-skeleton` and reaches `main` through a PR. Repo-sync isn't needed yet: there's no repo or sibling repos.

Out of the parent `dev-artemis/.claude/rules`, only the general rules apply here (PR card, assignee, no auto-reviewers). The Artemis-specific protocols don't apply: seed pipeline, ThinkingBlock, planner templates, `aol-us-shared` sync.

**Effort:** within a session. It's about 30 file edits and 1 PR, plus about 2 minutes of CI.

## 4. Decisions I need from you before setting up

1. **GitHub repo:** creating it is outward-facing, so I'll ask first. Name it `todo-app`, public or private? Until you say, I'll only `git init` locally.
2. **Frontend package manager:** the skeleton uses Bun, but a grader's Mac probably has Node and not Bun. I'd go with **npm**, plus `docker compose up` as the one-command run path, so "we can run it" never depends on extra installs. Or we keep Bun.
3. **`.env.example` is blocked:** the env and secrets hooks block it even though it holds no secrets, so I can't create the file that documents config. I'd add a narrow exception for `*.example` files only.
4. **Rule conflicts:**
   - **"How long would it have taken" in the README:** our time-estimation rule bans human-hours. That rule exists to set our own pace; the README is for outside graders who expect a human-time answer. I'd give agent-pair bounded work plus a solo-human equivalent, labelled as such.
   - **PR labels:** your workspace rule wants a label derived from the branch prefix, but the skeleton says no label. I'd add a branch-prefix-to-label table to CONTRIBUTING so both are satisfied.

I'll wait for your go-ahead and answers. The product decisions (auth design, ordering model, search, storage, deploy target) come in the spec and plan phase after the skeleton.

    return out

content.text: Now the rules. These three load every session: working agreement, coding standards and testing. Testing is now unscoped because TDD is a hard requirement.

input.content:
# Working agreement

How this team works with Claude Code. Applies to every session in this repo.

- Write in plain English: chat, docs, commit messages, PR text, code comments. Short sentences. If a simpler word carries the same meaning, use it.
- Lead with the answer or the outcome. Supporting detail comes after; leave out steps that do not change what the reader does next. Bullets for parallel items.
- Plan, align, execute. For anything beyond a small change, state the approach in a few lines and get a yes before building. Ask when different readings of the task would lead to different work. Do not ask about routine choices.
- Estimate in agent-pair time, not human-solo time. A well-aligned agent and human pair finishes in roughly a twentieth of the solo-human time. Give estimates as bounded work ("4 file edits, 1 migration, 1 PR" or "within a session"), never as human days. Name external waits (CI, deploys, reviews) separately.
- At the start of a session, run `/repo-sync` before writing code. Never switch or pull a repo that has uncommitted work without saying so.
- Stay in scope. Change only what the task names. Unrelated problems become a one-line follow-up note, not an inline fix.
- When a written plan or spec and the situation disagree, stop and ask. Never deviate silently, even when the deviation looks like an improvement. The spec for this repo is `docs/kickoff.md`, then the plan docs in `docs/plans/`.
- Report outcomes as they are. Failing tests are reported as failing, with output. Skipped steps are named. "Done" means `/verify` passed.
- The session transcript is shared with the reviewers as the record of how AI was used. Do the work inside the session: run the red test, then the green one, where the transcript shows both. Keep the human's decisions and the agent's work easy to tell apart.
- Keep the Claude Code files true to the code. Before a PR, `/claude-docs-check` reads the branch diff against `.claude/skills/claude-docs-check/map.json` and updates CLAUDE.md or the mapped rule on Opus, or records why not. A hook blocks `gh pr create` until that decision is on the branch.
- Before opening a PR, run `/raise-pr` and wait for a yes. One PR per branch.

# Coding standards

Applies to `backend/` (Python) and `frontend/` (TypeScript). The path-scoped rules add the language detail.

## General
- Minimal code. No speculative abstractions. No options nobody asked for.
- Concise but descriptive. A name says what a thing is or does; a reader should not need the comment to follow the code.
- Prefer editing an existing file to adding one. Delete what is unused. No dead branches.
- Every public function, class, component and type carries a one-line summary in the language's doc format (Google-style docstrings in Python, JSDoc in TypeScript). Sections (`Args:`, `@param`) only when they add something the signature does not say. Other comments are single line and only where the code cannot say it. No comment blocks. No commented-out code.
- Every change is verifiable. If you cannot test it, say so before shipping it.
- Match the surrounding code's style, not its gaps.

## Functional and declarative style (a hard requirement)
- Functional core, imperative shell. Domain logic (validation, ordering, search filters, mapping rows to responses) is pure functions with no I/O. Routers, repositories and React components are the thin shell that does I/O and calls the core.
- Never mutate an input. Return a new value. Python: frozen dataclasses, Pydantic models with `frozen=True` where they flow through the core, tuples over lists for fixed data. TypeScript: `const`, `readonly`, spread, `toSorted`/`toSpliced`/`with` over `sort`/`splice`.
- Prefer expressions to statements: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, comprehensions and generator expressions over loops that append into an accumulator. Use a loop only when it reads more clearly, and never just to mutate an outer variable.
- Compose small functions instead of writing one long one. Higher-order functions where they remove repetition: FastAPI `Depends` factories, decorators, hooks that take a query function, comparator builders. Do not add one for a single caller.
- Pick the data structure for the access pattern: a dict or `Map` for lookup by id, a set for membership, a list or tuple for order. Say why in review when it is not obvious.
- No hidden shared mutable state: no module-level caches that requests write to, no singletons holding request data.

## Async and concurrency (a hard requirement)
- Use the high-level abstraction, never hand-rolled threads or callbacks. Backend: `async def` handlers, the async SQLAlchemy session, `asyncio.TaskGroup` (or `gather`) when independent awaits can run together. Frontend: TanStack Query for all server state (caching, retries, cancellation, optimistic updates with rollback), never `useEffect` plus `fetch`.
- Never block the event loop. CPU-heavy work (password hashing) runs through `asyncio.to_thread` or the library's async API.

## Boundaries and types
- Every value that crosses a boundary (HTTP body, database row, token claims, storage, URL params) is a typed model, validated right after it is read: Pydantic in Python, Zod in TypeScript. Field access happens on the validated value. No `dict[str, Any]`, `any` or `Record<string, unknown>` for a known shape.
- Type hints on every parameter and return value, tests included. TypeScript is `strict`; no `any`, no `as unknown as`, no `@ts-ignore`.

## Logging
- Logs exist to monitor the running app and find bugs. Keep every line that does that: startup and ready, shutdown, a caught exception with its context, a request that failed auth or validation at WARNING, a degraded path taken.
- Remove every line added only to chase a bug during development before the commit. A log line that would not help someone on call is noise.
- Backend: `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`, never `print`. Frontend: `console.info` for lifecycle, `console.warn` and `console.error` for failures; never `console.log` or `console.debug`. ESLint enforces the frontend list.
- WARNING and ERROR lines say where, why and what happens next, with ids as key=value (`user_id=`, `task_id=`, `request_id=`). Never log secrets, passwords, tokens or full request bodies.

## Hygiene
- No `TODO`, `FIXME`, `XXX` or `HACK` in code. A follow-up goes in the PR description or an issue.
- No `debugger`, `breakpoint()`, `pdb`, or focused tests (`.only`). `scripts/check-hygiene.sh` checks all of this and runs in CI and in `/verify`.
- Secrets never appear in code, logs, tests, or chat. `.env` files and key material are off limits; a hook enforces this. Anything bundled into the frontend is public.

# Testing

Robust testing is a hard requirement, and so is test-driven development. Applies to every change.

## Test first
- Red, green, refactor. Write the test, run it and watch it fail for the expected reason, write the least code that makes it pass, then clean up with the test still green. Run the red step in the session so the transcript shows it.
- Every commit is green. All suites that the change touches pass before `git commit`; a failing test is never committed. A commit holds the test and the code that passes it together.
- New behaviour gets a test in the same commit. A bug fix starts with a test that reproduces the bug.

## Each layer earns its place
Test a behaviour once, at the lowest layer that can catch it. A higher layer covers only what the lower layers cannot see. Before adding a test, name the failure it catches that no existing test catches; if there is none, do not add it.

| Layer | Tool | Owns | Does not re-test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backend unit | pytest | pure functions in the core: ordering, search filters, validation, token and password helpers | anything HTTP or SQL |
| Backend integration | pytest, httpx `ASGITransport`, a real database | each endpoint's contract: status codes, response shape, auth, ownership, persistence | the pure rules already unit-tested, beyond one case that proves the wiring |
| Frontend unit and component | Vitest (its API matches Jest's), React Testing Library, MSW at the `fetch` boundary | pure helpers, hooks, and each screen's states: loading, empty, error, success, validation | backend rules |
| Live-server e2e | pytest against the running stack (compose, then k3d) | what only a deployed stack shows: migrations ran, config and CORS, ingress and routing, a token issued by one replica accepted by another | endpoint contracts |
| Browser e2e | Playwright against the running stack | a few complete user journeys: sign in, create, reorder, search, edit, delete, sign out; and the small-screen layout | screen states and endpoint contracts |

## Mechanics
- Mock at the boundary (the HTTP client, `fetch`, the clock), never inside the code under test. Nothing in a unit suite opens a socket.
- Tests are independent and order-free. Each builds its own data through factories or fixtures; none relies on another's leftovers.
- Assert on behaviour a user or caller can see: status, body, rendered text and roles. Never on private attributes or CSS class names.
- One reason to fail per test. The name says the behaviour: `test_reorder_rejects_task_owned_by_another_user`, `it("shows the empty state when the user has no tasks")`.
- Coverage is a floor, not a target: CI fails below the threshold set in `pyproject.toml` and `vitest.config.ts`. A line covered by a test that asserts nothing is not covered.
- Report results as they are. "128 passed" means you saw it. Name the suite and the stack it ran against.

# Git and pull requests

## Branches
- Work on a branch off `main`: `feature/<name>`, `fix/<name>`, `chore/<name>`, `docs/<name>`, `refactor/<name>`, `perf/<name>`, `test/<name>`, `ci/<name>`. Lowercase, hyphens, no personal names.
- Never commit on `main`. Never force-push a shared branch. Never `--no-verify`. A hook blocks all three.
- Releases are `vX.Y.Z` tags on `main`. A tag is never moved or deleted; a wrong tag is fixed by cutting the next version. A hook blocks tag moves.

## Commits
- One logical change per commit, and every commit is green (see `testing.md`). Conventional Commits: `type(scope): subject`. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert, release. Scopes: `api`, `web`, `db`, `auth`, `deploy`, `claude`, or none. Subject starts lowercase, no trailing period, imperative mood.
- The body says why, not what.
- Add `Refs: #<issue>` or `Refs: docs/plans/<file>.md` when there is one.

## Pull requests
- Run `/raise-pr`. It shows the card (title, branch, base, assignee, label, summary) and waits for a yes.
- The title follows the commit format. A hook blocks titles that do not.
- Assignee is the human whose git identity is on the commits. No reviewers unless the human names them.
- Label: exactly one, taken from the branch prefix through the table in `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2. A prefix with no row in that table is a gap; ask before raising.
- Description: what, why, how to test, risks and rollback. Link sources instead of restating them.
- Merge: squash-and-merge. The reviewer has the final call.
- `git push` and `gh pr create` always ask before running. That is intended.

# Python

## Boundaries and types
- Pydantic models at every boundary: request and response bodies, database rows leaving the repository layer, token claims. `Model.model_validate(raw)` right after deserializing; field access happens on the model.
- Request and response models are separate types (`TaskCreate`, `TaskUpdate`, `TaskRead`). A response never exposes a column the client should not see, such as a password hash.
- Settings are one pydantic-settings class. With `extra="ignore"` a typo in an env var name fails silently, so check the name when a value is missing.
- `X | None` and `dict[str, X]`. `Mapping` and `Sequence` for parameters you only read. A frozen dataclass or TypedDict for a value that stays inside the service; a Pydantic model for anything that crosses a boundary.

## Docstrings

# API contract

The REST contract between `backend/` and `frontend/`. Change both sides in the same PR, or neither.

- Resources are nouns under `/api/v1`: `/auth/...`, `/tasks`, `/tasks/{id}`. Standard methods: `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PATCH` updates part of a resource, `DELETE` removes. JSON in and out.
- Status codes:

| Case | Code |
|---|---|
| Read or update succeeded | 200 |
| Created; the response carries the resource and a `Location` header | 201 |
| Deleted | 204, no body |
| Body or query fails validation | **400** (FastAPI's default is 422; the app maps `RequestValidationError` to 400 in one handler) |
| No token, bad token, expired token, wrong password | 401 |
| Authenticated but not allowed to do this action | 403 |
| Resource missing, **or owned by another user** (so ids of other users' tasks are never confirmed) | 404 |
| Conflict with current state, such as a username already taken | 409 |

- Every error body has one shape, a typed model: `{"error": {"code": "...", "message": "...", "details": [...]}}`. `code` is a stable machine string the frontend switches on; `message` is safe to show a user.
- List endpoints return a typed envelope, not a bare array, so paging can be added without breaking clients.
- The frontend parses every response with a Zod schema that mirrors the backend's Pydantic model. When a model changes, the schema changes in the same PR, and the integration test for that endpoint asserts the new shape.
- Every endpoint has an integration test for its success code and each error code it can return.

# TypeScript

- `strict` is on in `tsconfig.json`. No `any`, no `as unknown as`, no `@ts-ignore`, no non-null `!` to silence a real `undefined`. Named exports. Function components with hooks; no classes.
- Every boundary is a Zod schema under `src/lib/schema/`: API responses, form data, storage, URL params. `parse`, or `safeParse` with a typed error path, right after reading; field access on the parsed value. Types come from the schema with `z.infer`, never written twice.
- Every API call goes through the one fetch wrapper in `src/lib/api/`, which attaches the token, parses the body and turns error bodies into a typed `ApiError`. No bare `fetch` in components or hooks.
- Domain types live in `src/types/` or next to their schema, reachable from any layer. Never define a cross-cutting type inside `components/`.
- Enums are `as const` objects, not `enum`. Use the typed constant, never the string literal.
- Discriminated unions are closed. Switch on the discriminant, and make the switch exhaustive with a `never` check.
- Environment values are read through one module, never raw `import.meta.env` in components. Build-time values are public; a secret never goes there.
- JSDoc: a summary line on every exported function, component and type. `@param` and `@returns` only when they say something the signature does not.
- Logic lives in exported pure helpers a test can reach (filtering, ordering, formatting), not inline in markup.
- Filenames are kebab-case. Tests sit next to the code they test as `<name>.test.ts(x)`.
- `npm run check` (ESLint, Prettier check, `tsc --noEmit`) is the gate.

# React

- Function components with hooks. Every hook is declared before any conditional `return`; hooks run in the same order every render. `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` and `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` are errors.
- Server state lives in TanStack Query, and only there. Each resource has one module of query keys and hooks (`useTasks`, `useUpdateTask`); components never build query keys inline. Mutations that the user should see at once (reorder, toggle, delete) are optimistic, roll back on error and show the error.
- `useState` is for local affordances only: an open menu, a draft form value. Auth state is one context. Never copy server data into local state.
- Derive, do not mirror. A value computed from props or query data is computed during render (with `useMemo` only when it is measurably costly), never stored by an effect. `useEffect` is for syncing with something outside React, not for data flow.
- Forms validate with the same Zod schema the API layer uses, and show errors next to the field.
- Responsive by default, mobile first: Tailwind utilities, layouts that work from 320px wide up, touch targets of at least 44px, reorder that works by touch and by keyboard as well as by mouse.
- Accessible by default: real buttons and links, a label on every input, visible focus, and roles and names that tests query by.
- Styling: Tailwind utilities first. Inline `style` only for values the utility layer cannot express.

# Deployment

## Stages, in order
1. **Containers**: each service builds its own image; `docker compose up` runs the stack (database, backend, frontend). The whole test pyramid passes here first.
2. **Local Kubernetes**: a k3d cluster runs the same images from the same manifests, with more than one backend replica. Development continues here once stage 1 is proven.
3. **AKS**: an Azure Kubernetes Service cluster, deployed by GitHub Actions, only after stage 2 works end to end and the human signs off.

Do not start a stage before the previous one is proven and the human says go.

## The human reviews every deployment artifact
- Dockerfiles, compose files, Kubernetes manifests, overlays and workflows are shown to the human and approved before they are applied or merged. Show the file and say what it will create or change.
- The agent never applies anything to AKS or any shared cloud resource. It prepares the change and the exact command; the human runs it (`CONTRIBUTING.md` § 11). `kubectl apply`, `kubectl delete`, `helm` and `az` always ask, even against k3d.

## Built for more than one replica
- The backend is stateless: auth is a signed token checked on every request, with no in-memory sessions or caches that requests write to. Any replica can serve any request.
- One set of manifests (Kustomize base) with one overlay per target (`k3d`, `aks`). No copy-pasted manifests per environment.
- Images are tagged with the git sha, never `latest`, and the same image moves from one stage to the next.
- Migrations run once per release as a Job before the backend rolls out, never from every pod at startup.
- Every backend pod has a liveness probe (`/healthz`, process up) and a readiness probe (`/readyz`, database reachable). Requests and limits are set. Containers run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem where the runtime allows.
- Config comes from env vars through ConfigMaps; secrets come from Kubernetes Secrets the human creates. Neither is ever committed.

# Git and pull requests

## Branches
- Work on a branch off `main`: `feature/<name>`, `fix/<name>`, `chore/<name>`, `docs/<name>`, `refactor/<name>`, `perf/<name>`, `test/<name>`, `ci/<name>`. Lowercase, hyphens, no personal names.
- Never commit on `main`. Never force-push a shared branch. Never `--no-verify`. A hook blocks all three.
- Releases are `vX.Y.Z` tags on `main`. A tag is never moved or deleted; a wrong tag is fixed by cutting the next version. A hook blocks tag moves.

## Commits
- One logical change per commit, and every commit is green (see `testing.md`). Conventional Commits: `type(scope): subject`. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert, release. Scopes: `api`, `web`, `db`, `auth`, `deploy`, `claude`, or none. Subject starts lowercase, no trailing period, imperative mood.
- The body says why, not what.
- Add `Refs: #<issue>` or `Refs: docs/plans/<file>.md` when there is one.

## Pull requests
- Run `/raise-pr`. It shows the card (title, branch, base, assignee, label, summary) and waits for a yes.
- The title follows the commit format. A hook blocks titles that do not.
- Assignee is the human whose git identity is on the commits. No reviewers unless the human names them.
- Label: exactly one, taken from the branch prefix through the table in `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2. A prefix with no row in that table is a gap; ask before raising.
- Description: what, why, how to test, risks and rollback. Link sources instead of restating them.
- Merge: squash-and-merge. The reviewer has the final call.
- `git push` and `gh pr create` always ask before running. That is intended.

# Deployment

## Stages, in order
1. **Containers**: each service builds its own image; `docker compose up` runs the stack (database, backend, frontend). The whole test pyramid passes here first.
2. **Local Kubernetes**: a k3d cluster runs the same images from the same manifests, with more than one backend replica. Development continues here once stage 1 is proven.
3. **AKS**: an Azure Kubernetes Service cluster, deployed by GitHub Actions, only after stage 2 works end to end and the human signs off.

Do not start a stage before the previous one is proven and the human says go.

## The human reviews every deployment artifact
- Dockerfiles, compose files, Kubernetes manifests, overlays and workflows are shown to the human and approved before they are applied or merged. Show the file and say what it will create or change.
- The agent never applies anything to AKS or any shared cloud resource. It prepares the change and the exact command; the human runs it (`CONTRIBUTING.md` § 11). `kubectl apply`, `kubectl delete`, `helm` and `az` always ask, even against k3d.

## Built for more than one replica
- The backend is stateless: auth is a signed token checked on every request, with no in-memory sessions or caches that requests write to. Any replica can serve any request.
- One set of manifests (Kustomize base) with one overlay per target (`k3d`, `aks`). No copy-pasted manifests per environment.
- Images are tagged with the git sha, never `latest`, and the same image moves from one stage to the next.
- Migrations run once per release as a Job before the backend rolls out, never from every pod at startup.
- Every backend pod has a liveness probe (`/healthz`, process up) and a readiness probe (`/readyz`, database reachable). Requests and limits are set. Containers run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem where the runtime allows.
- Config comes from env vars through ConfigMaps; secrets come from Kubernetes Secrets the human creates. Neither is ever committed.

name: reviewer
description: Adversarial reviewer for a branch or PR. Use before a human reads the diff. Finds correctness bugs, scope creep, missing or redundant tests and rule violations, then writes up the assumptions the author made.
model: opus
memory: project
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash

You review code written by another agent or a person. You have not seen their conversation, so you do not share their blind spots. Be specific and be fair.

Input: a branch name or a PR number. Start with `git diff origin/main...<branch>` or `gh pr diff <n>`.

Cover all of:
1. Correctness. Does each hunk do what the commit message says? Trace inputs to outputs for anything that crosses a boundary, and read the receiving side's types. For the API: the status code for every error path matches `api-contract.md`, and every task query filters on the owner.
2. Scope. Anything in the diff the task did not ask for? Name it.
3. Tests. New behaviour without a test, a test that cannot fail, and a test that repeats what another layer already proves (`testing.md`, "Each layer earns its place"). Check that each commit is green on its own.
4. Style. Functional core and imperative shell: pure domain logic, no mutated inputs, `map`/`filter`/`reduce` and comprehensions over accumulator loops, composition over long functions, the right data structure for the access pattern. Async through the high-level abstraction (async SQLAlchemy, `TaskGroup`, TanStack Query), never `useEffect` plus `fetch`.
5. Rules. Read `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/` and check the diff against them. Backend: Pydantic at every boundary, full type hints with no open `dict` or `Any`, migrations only through alembic, no network call at import time. Frontend: strict TypeScript with no `any`, a Zod schema at every boundary, hooks before any early return, server state only in TanStack Query, responsive and accessible markup. Both: docstrings and JSDoc on every export, single-line comments, no dead code, no secrets.
6. Logging. Every log line helps someone monitor the app or find a bug. Flag lines left over from debugging, `print`, `console.log`, and any line that logs a secret or a full body.
7. Simplicity. Code that could be shorter or could reuse something that exists.

Output, in this order: findings ranked by severity, each with file, line and a one-line failure scenario; then the assumptions and design decisions you believe the author made, and why. One or two sentences per item; leave out anything that would not change what the author does next. Plain English.

Update your memory with recurring patterns you find in this repo, so the next review starts ahead. One pattern per entry with a one-line summary. Skip what CLAUDE.md and the rules already say, and fix entries that turn out to be wrong.

# Raise a PR

Do these steps in order. Stop after step 4 and wait.

1. Sync: `git fetch --all --prune`, then report behind/ahead against the base branch. Rebase if behind. With no remote yet, say so and skip.
2. Check the branch: every commit is on a branch off `main`, the tree is clean, and `/verify` has passed. Run `/claude-docs-check`; the PR hook blocks `gh pr create` until its decision is on the branch.
3. Build the card:
   - Title: `type(scope): subject`. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert, release. Subject starts lowercase, no trailing period.
   - Branch and base (usually `main`).
   - Assignee: the GitHub login of the human whose git identity is on the commits. `git log -1 --format=%an` gives the name; `gh api user --jq .login` confirms the login.
   - Label: one, from the branch prefix through `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2. If the label does not exist on the repo yet (`gh label list`), say so on the card; creating it is part of the yes.
   - Summary: one to three lines. The problem and the chosen approach.
   - Description with the sections What, Why, How to test, Risks and rollback. Link sources rather than restating them. End with the attribution footer the session gives you.
4. Show the card and the description in chat. Ask for a go. Do not push or create anything yet.
5. On a yes: create the label if the card said it was missing, `git push -u origin <branch>`, then `gh pr create --base <base> --head <branch> --title "<title>" --body-file <file> --assignee <login> --label <label>`. The commands prompt for permission; that is expected.
6. Report the PR URL, then `gh pr checks <n> --watch` and report the result.

Never add reviewers unless the human names them. Never open a second PR for the same branch.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Fail when shipped code carries task markers, debugger hooks, focused tests or debug-only logging.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"

code=(backend frontend e2e deploy ':!*.lock' ':!*lock.json' ':!**/node_modules/**' ':!**/.venv/**')
python=(backend ':!backend/tests/**')
typescript=(frontend/src e2e ':!**/node_modules/**')
tests=(frontend/src e2e backend/tests)

checks=(
  "task marker|\\b(TODO|FIXME|XXX|HACK)\\b|code"
  "python debugger|\\bbreakpoint\\(|\\bpdb\\b|python"
  "print in backend code (use logging)|^\\s*print\\(|python"
  "typescript debugger|\\bdebugger\\b|typescript"
  "debug-only console call (use console.info, warn or error)|console\\.(log|debug|trace)\\(|typescript"
  "focused or skipped-by-default test|\\b(it|test|describe)\\.only\\(|tests"
)

failed=0
for check in "${checks[@]}"; do
  IFS='|' read -r label pattern scope <<<"$check"
  declare -n paths="$scope"
  if hits=$(git grep -nIP --untracked --exclude-standard -e "$pattern" -- "${paths[@]}" 2>/dev/null); then
    printf '%s:\n%s\n\n' "$label" "$hits"
    failed=1
  fi
done

if ((failed)); then
  echo "hygiene check failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "hygiene check passed"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Fail when shipped code carries task markers, debugger hooks, focused tests or debug-only logging.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"

code=(backend frontend e2e deploy ':!*.lock' ':!*lock.json' ':!**/node_modules/**' ':!**/.venv/**')
python=(backend ':!backend/tests/**')
typescript=(frontend/src e2e ':!**/node_modules/**')
tests=(frontend/src e2e backend/tests)

checks=(
  "task marker|\\b(TODO|FIXME|XXX|HACK)\\b|code"
  "python debugger|\\bbreakpoint\\(|\\bpdb\\b|python"
  "print in backend code (use logging)|^\\s*print\\(|python"
  "typescript debugger|\\bdebugger\\b|typescript"
  "debug-only console call (use console.info, warn or error)|console\\.(log|debug|trace)\\(|typescript"
  "focused or skipped-by-default test|\\b(it|test|describe)\\.only\\(|tests"
)

failed=0
for check in "${checks[@]}"; do
  IFS='|' read -r label pattern scope <<<"$check"
  declare -n paths="$scope"
  if hits=$(git grep -nIP --untracked --exclude-standard -e "$pattern" -- "${paths[@]}" 2>/dev/null); then
    printf '%s:\n%s\n\n' "$label" "$hits"
    failed=1
  fi
done

  echo "hygiene check failed" >&2

```
feature/<name>      ←  you work here, branched off main
       │
       │  GATE — every suite passes on this branch (§ 5)
       ▼
       PR  →  main   ←  squash-merged after review
       │
       ▼

```

**Never push directly to `main`.** Always go through a PR. A wrong tag is fixed by cutting the next version, never by moving the existing one.

Deployment moves through three stages, each proven before the next starts: containers with `docker compose`, then a local k3d cluster, then AKS through GitHub Actions. `.claude/rules/deployment.md` holds the details. s2 = """## 2. Branch naming and PR labels

- Lowercase with hyphens. No spaces, no underscores, no camelCase, no personal names.
- Prefix with type. Short and descriptive: what the branch *does*, not who is doing it.

✓ Good: `feature/task-reorder` · `fix/token-expiry-401` · `docs/readme-deploy`
✗ Bad:  `my-branch` · `Fix-Login-Alex` · `main-2` · `feature/everything`

Every PR carries exactly one label, taken from its branch prefix:

| Branch prefix | Label |
|---|---|
| `feature/` | `enhancement` |
| `fix/` | `bug` |
| `docs/` | `documentation` |
| `chore/` | `chore` |
| `refactor/` | `refactor` |
| `perf/` | `performance` |
| `test/` | `test` |
| `ci/` | `ci` |

A prefix that is not in this table is a gap: add a row in the same PR, after asking.

"""

**Before every commit and before opening a PR**, from the repo root, for each part the change touched:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py                                     # no task markers, debuggers, focused tests or debug-only logs

```

"""

"""

Path("CONTRIBUTING.md").write_text(out)

# todo-app

A full-stack To Do list for an engineering challenge. A user signs in and manages only their own tasks: create, read, update, delete, reorder and search, with a detail screen per task and a responsive UI. `backend/` is a REST API in Python (FastAPI, async SQLAlchemy, alembic, Postgres). `frontend/` is a React SPA in TypeScript (Vite, TanStack Query, Zod, Tailwind). The app is built to run as more than one backend replica: containers first, then a local k3d cluster, then AKS.

## Read first
- `docs/kickoff.md`: the requirements, the human's feedback and the locked decisions. It is the spec; plans in `docs/plans/` build on it.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`: branches and deploy stages (§1), branch names and PR labels (§2), test gates (§5), the kind-stop protocol (§8), human-runs-it for ops and deploys (§11), secrets (§12).
- `.claude/rules/`: working agreement, coding standards, testing and git rules load every session. Python, database, API contract, TypeScript, React and deployment rules load when you touch matching files.
- `backend/CLAUDE.md` and `frontend/CLAUDE.md`: each app's commands, config and layout.
- Skills: `/repo-sync` at the start of a session, `/verify` before saying done or committing, `/claude-docs-check` then `/raise-pr` to open a PR.

## Hard requirements that shape every change
- Test-driven: red, green, refactor, and every commit is green. Each test layer owns different failures; no test repeats another layer's job (`testing.md`).
- Functional and declarative: a pure core with an I/O shell, no mutated inputs, composition and higher-order functions, `map`/`filter`/`reduce` and comprehensions, the right data structure (`coding-standards.md`).
- Async through high-level abstractions: async FastAPI and SQLAlchemy with `TaskGroup` on the backend, TanStack Query on the frontend.
- Logs that help monitoring stay (startup, ready, caught errors with context); logs added only to debug go before the commit. No `TODO` or `FIXME` in code.
- HTTP semantics as in `api-contract.md`, including 400 (not FastAPI's default 422) for validation errors and 404 for another user's task.

## Commands
```bash
python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py      # task markers, debuggers, focused tests, debug-only logs; CI runs it
```
Each app's own commands are in its `CLAUDE.md`; `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 5 lists every gate.

## Config and secrets
- Never read or edit `.env` files, `.env.example` or key material. Hooks and the deny list block it, and a Bash command that only names such a file is blocked too. When a setting is needed, post the exact lines in chat and the human adds them.
- `.mcp.json` configures Claude Code's own MCP servers. It is not the app's config.

## Workspace rules
This repo sits inside a larger workspace whose `.claude/rules/` also load. The general rules there apply (PR card, assignee, no auto-reviewers, typed boundaries, failure handling). The product-specific protocols do not: seed compile and migrate, planner templates, ThinkingBlock, user cleanup scripts, turbo logs, and sibling contract repos. There are no sibling repos here.

## Gotchas
- macOS ships bash 3.2. Repo scripts are Python 3 standard library, like the hooks, so they run on a reviewer's Mac and in CI.
- The branch-protection hook blocks every commit on `main`. Branch first.
- FastAPI answers validation errors with 422 unless the app's handler maps them. Keep the handler; the contract says 400.

## Branches and deploy
- Work on a branch off `main`. PR to `main`, squash-merge. Releases are `vX.Y.Z` tags; a tag is never moved.
- CI runs on every PR: hygiene, plus the backend and frontend gates as those apps land.
- Deploy stages are in `.claude/rules/deployment.md`. The human reviews every deployment artifact before it is applied, and runs anything against AKS.
- Guards: a hook blocks commits and pushes on `main`, force pushes, `--no-verify` and tag moves. `git push`, `gh pr create`, `kubectl apply`/`delete`, `helm` and `az` always ask. PR titles must be Conventional Commits. A PR also needs a docs decision from `/claude-docs-check`.

## Scope
Change only what the task names. Do not fix nearby code or add tests the change does not need. Unrelated problems go in a one-line follow-up note.

A user signs in and manages only their own tasks: create, read, update, delete, reorder and search, with a detail screen per task and a responsive UI. `backend/` is a REST API in Python (FastAPI, async SQLAlchemy, alembic, Postgres). `frontend/` is a React SPA in TypeScript (Vite, TanStack Query, Zod, Tailwind). The app is built to run as more than one backend replica: containers first, then a local k3d cluster, then AKS.

## Read first
- `docs/kickoff.md`: the requirements, the human's feedback and the locked decisions. It is the spec; plans in `docs/plans/` build on it.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`: branches and deploy stages (§1), branch names and PR labels (§2), test gates (§5), the kind-stop protocol (§8), human-runs-it for ops and deploys (§11), secrets (§12).
- `.claude/rules/`: working agreement, coding standards, testing and git rules load every session. Python, database, API contract, TypeScript, React and deployment rules load when you touch matching files.
- `backend/CLAUDE.md` and `frontend/CLAUDE.md`: each app's commands, config and layout.
- Skills: `/repo-sync` at the start of a session, `/verify` before saying done or committing, `/claude-docs-check` then `/raise-pr` to open a PR.

## Hard requirements that shape every change
- Test-driven: red, green, refactor, and every commit is green. Each test layer owns different failures; no test repeats another layer's job (`testing.md`).
- Functional and declarative: a pure core with an I/O shell, no mutated inputs, composition and higher-order functions, `map`/`filter`/`reduce` and comprehensions, the right data structure (`coding-standards.md`).
- Async through high-level abstractions: async FastAPI and SQLAlchemy with `TaskGroup` on the backend, TanStack Query on the frontend.
- Logs that help monitoring stay (startup, ready, caught errors with context); logs added only to debug go before the commit. No `TODO` or `FIXME` in code.
- HTTP semantics as in `api-contract.md`, including 400 (not FastAPI's default 422) for validation errors and 404 for another user's task.

## Commands
```bash
python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py      # task markers, debuggers, focused tests, debug-only logs; CI runs it
```
Each app's own commands are in its `CLAUDE.md`; `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 5 lists every gate.

## Config and secrets
- Never read or edit `.env` files, `.env.example` or key material. Hooks and the deny list block it, and a Bash command that only names such a file is blocked too. When a setting is needed, post the exact lines in chat and the human adds them.
- `.mcp.json` configures Claude Code's own MCP servers. It is not the app's config.

## Workspace rules
This repo sits inside a larger workspace whose `.claude/rules/` also load. The general rules there apply (PR card, assignee, no auto-reviewers, typed boundaries, failure handling). The product-specific protocols do not: seed compile and migrate, planner templates, ThinkingBlock, user cleanup scripts, turbo logs, and sibling contract repos. There are no sibling repos here.

## Gotchas
- macOS ships bash 3.2. Repo scripts are Python 3 standard library, like the hooks, so they run on a reviewer's Mac and in CI.
- The branch-protection hook blocks every commit on `main`. Branch first.
- FastAPI answers validation errors with 422 unless the app's handler maps them. Keep the handler; the contract says 400.

## Branches and deploy
- Work on a branch off `main`. PR to `main`, squash-merge. Releases are `vX.Y.Z` tags; a tag is never moved.
- CI runs on every PR: hygiene, plus the backend and frontend gates as those apps land.
- Deploy stages are in `.claude/rules/deployment.md`. The human reviews every deployment artifact before it is applied, and runs anything against AKS.
- Guards: a hook blocks commits and pushes on `main`, force pushes, `--no-verify` and tag moves. `git push`, `gh pr create`, `kubectl apply`/`delete`, `helm` and `az` always ask. PR titles must be Conventional Commits. A PR also needs a docs decision from `/claude-docs-check`.

## Scope
Change only what the task names. Do not fix nearby code or add tests the change does not need. Unrelated problems go in a one-line follow-up note.

# Kickoff — requirements, feedback and decisions

The spec for this repo. Written 2026-10-18 at the start of the first session, after the challenge brief was read and reviewed with the human lead. Plans in `docs/plans/` build on it; when a plan and this file disagree, stop and ask.

## 1. What we are building

A full-stack To Do list: a web client and our own backend API. A user signs in and does full CRUD on their own tasks, and only their own.

| Area | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Backend | A REST-style API: resource URLs, standard methods, JSON. Status codes: 200/201 success, 400 validation, 401/403 auth, 404 missing. |
| Frontend | Connects to our API. Sign-in landing page, task list after sign-in, reorder, search, a task detail screen to view and edit, full CRUD. Responsive. |
| README | Running on a Mac; deployment to distributed cloud infrastructure; overall approach; features completed; what we would add with more time and how long it would take; what we would do to make it more robust. |
| Code | In a shareable git repo, runnable by the reviewers, community-standard style, no debug-only logging, no `TODO` or `FIXME`, tested. |
| Style and practice | Clean code, concise but descriptive. Test-driven. Functional and declarative (higher-order functions, composition, `map`/`filter`/`reduce`, the right data structures). Async through high-level abstractions. |

Missing the minimum criteria ends the interview, so "the reviewers can run it" comes first, and every design choice must be one we can explain in a live deep-dive.

## 2. The human lead's feedback (verbatim) and what it means for the work

> 1. TBH, one thing to keep in mind is that the Bonus note on `TDD. Functional, declarative style (higher-order functions, composition, map/filter/reduce, correct data structures). Async through high-level abstractions.` is not a Bonus. Consider it an ALL IN Hard req.

TDD, functional style and high-level async are hard requirements, written into `coding-standards.md`, `testing.md` and the reviewer agent.

> 2. Great catch on the vald status code.

FastAPI's default 422 for validation errors is mapped to 400 in one handler (`api-contract.md`).

> 3. On the debug logging note: Logs are fine, just ensure we don't have any logs that you added just to debug errors that popped up along the way and ensure every print/console adds value to monitoring for bugs. So for example, printing exception errors, etc is absolutely needed, printing status ready for components/app is needed. I just don't want you to assume that absolutely no logging is allowed. That is not the case here.

Logging stays where it helps monitoring: lifecycle (startup, ready, shutdown), caught exceptions with context, warnings on auth or validation failures and degraded paths. Lines added only to chase a bug are removed before the commit. Backend uses `logging`; frontend uses `console.info`, `warn` and `error`, never `log` or `debug` (`coding-standards.md`, enforced by ESLint and `scripts/check_hygiene.py`).

> 4. On testing frameworks, lets use Vitest and note down that the API matches JEST. also it feels like a general guidance to me that robust testing is an absolute requirement. All tests should be passing before we commit. Every test (unit, integration, live server e2e tests, and playwright tests) should all add unique value. I don't want redundancy across tests just for the sake of bloating our test scene.

Vitest on the frontend (its API matches Jest's; the README says so), pytest on the backend. Every commit is green. Five layers, each owning failures the others cannot see; a test that repeats another layer's job is not added (`testing.md`, "Each layer earns its place"). Red-then-green happens inside the session, so the shared transcript shows each failing run before the passing one, and each commit holds the test and the code together.

> 5. We'll deploy towards the end, but i think we should definitely deploy. We'll initially build and test with sep docker container. once proven that the app works and all functonality works as expected, code is reviewed and tests are run -> then, we'll test and run locally using kubernetes (we'll setup a k3d cluster since the task mentions a bonus for distributed deployment efforts...do you agree on this note?). and we'll deploy on an azure subscription where we'll have a AKS cluster setup. We could use github actions then for deployment. I want to review each of the deployment artifacts before we deploy. Additionally, we'll focus on development on a local k3d cluster. Once everything is proven and working seamlessly and meeting my expectations, we'll proceed with AKS later if time permits.

Agreed on k3d. It runs k3s, a certified Kubernetes, so the same manifests carry over to AKS with only an overlay per target, and it lets us prove the distributed parts on a laptop: several backend replicas behind a Service, a migration Job, probes, rolling updates. That forces the right design early: a stateless backend (signed tokens, no in-memory sessions) and a shared Postgres, never in-memory or file storage. Stages: separate containers with `docker compose` → local k3d → AKS through GitHub Actions if time permits. The human reviews every deployment artifact before it is applied (`deployment.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 11).

> 6. I also want to review all the coding instructions before we begin. Not now, after we write out the detailed coding plan, you'll walk me through the instruction in chat along with code samples, commenting style samples, type checking samples, etc.

A gate before any app code: after the detailed coding plan, a walkthrough in chat of every coding instruction, with code, comment-style and type-checking samples. Coding starts only after the human signs off.

> 7. I also want to save this chat's transcript. It possible to find the json file. I've done this in the past for another interview. We saved the file with transcript, timestamps and all other info. If we can share this with the interviewing team, that would resolve all their questions on my AI usage for completing this assessment.

Claude Code writes each session as JSONL, one event per line with a timestamp, under `~/.claude/projects/<encoded project path>/<session id>.jsonl`, with subagent runs in a folder of the same name. At the end we export the session files into `docs/ai-usage/`, scan them for secrets and personal details before they are committed, and derive the human-versus-agent time split from the timestamps (see decision 4).

> 8. Skeleton setup - OK

## 3. Locked decisions

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| 1 | The repository is `todo-app`, local for now, public on GitHub later. Creating the remote waits for the human's go. |
| 2 | The frontend uses Node and npm (no Bun), so the reviewers need nothing beyond Node, plus `docker compose up` as a one-command run. ESLint and Prettier for style. |
| 3 | The env and secrets hooks stay as they are, `.env.example` included. The agent posts the exact lines in chat and the human creates or edits the file. |
| 4 | The final report makes the split between human and agent work easy to see, derived from the transcript timestamps, alongside the agent-pair estimates the workspace rule asks for. |
| 5 | PRs carry one label taken from the branch prefix (`CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2). |
| 6 | One monorepo: `backend/`, `frontend/`, and later `e2e/` and `deploy/`, with one root `.claude/`. |
| 7 | The challenge brief (`TASK.md`) stays local and untracked; this file carries its requirements. |

## 4. Sequence and gates

1. Repo skeleton: the Claude Code setup adapted from the template repo and upgraded with the rules above. Pause for review.
2. Spec and detailed coding plan in `docs/plans/`: data model, auth, ordering, search, API endpoints, screens, test plan per layer, deployment shape.
3. **Gate:** walkthrough of the coding instructions with samples; the human signs off.
4. Build, test-first: backend, then frontend, then containers, with the human reviewing at regular points.
5. **Gate:** containers proven, code reviewed, every suite green → local k3d.
6. **Gate:** k3d proven and the human satisfied → AKS through GitHub Actions, if time permits. Every deployment artifact reviewed before it is applied.
7. README, the transcript export and the human-versus-agent time report.

## 5. Open for the spec phase

- Auth: how accounts exist (sign-up screen or seeded users), token format and lifetime, where the frontend keeps the token.
- Ordering: how positions are stored so a reorder is one cheap, consistent write.
- Search: server-side or client-side, which fields, and whether it combines with ordering.
- Task fields beyond title and done state (description, due date, priority).
- Deployment target details: ingress, the managed Postgres choice for AKS, and how images reach the cluster registry.

The skeleton is set up, verified and committed locally on `chore/repo-skeleton`; nothing is pushed and there's no remote yet. I've stopped here as you asked.

**On k3d: yes, I agree.** k3d runs real Kubernetes, so the same manifests carry over to AKS with one small override file per target. It also lets us prove the distributed parts on your laptop: several backend replicas, a one-off migration job, health checks. It forces the right design early, too: a backend that keeps no session state (signed tokens) and a shared Postgres database instead of in-memory or file storage.

**Your feedback is in `docs/kickoff.md`**, quoted word for word, with what each point means for the work. It also has the locked decisions, the review gates (including your walkthrough of the coding instructions before any app code) and the questions left for the spec phase.
