Many users at once · FastAPI and uvicorn

Async and concurrency

Each API replica is one uvicorn process running one event loop. The loop can hold thousands of open requests, but only while each of them is waiting on I/O. Anything that keeps the loop busy (a slow hash, a blocking call, a synchronous write) stalls every request on that replica at once. So the design has three jobs: never block the loop, put a limit on every shared resource, and when a limit is reached, make requests queue for a bounded time or get a clear 503 rather than pile up.

D13

One uvicorn process per container, every handler async

your call
Choice
uvicorn[standard] (uvloop, httptools) with one worker per container; more capacity means more replicas. Every route is async def and uses only async libraries. --limit-concurrency 200 answers 503 past 200 in-flight requests. --timeout-graceful-shutdown 20 lets in-flight requests finish on SIGTERM, then the lifespan closes the pool. Nginx keeps connections to the API open and caps request bodies at 64 KB.
Instead of
Gunicorn or uvicorn managing several worker processes inside one container. Or plain def handlers, which FastAPI runs on a thread pool capped at 40 threads by default.
Why
One process per container lets Docker and Kubernetes restart it, count it and scale it, and each pod's memory and CPU stay predictable. Async-only handlers mean the loop is the only scheduler to reason about.
D14

Password hashing runs off the loop, at most four at a time

your call
Choice
argon2id with OWASP's parameters (19 MiB memory, 2 passes, 1 lane), run through asyncio.to_thread behind an asyncio.Semaphore(4) per process. argon2-cffi releases the GIL while it hashes, so the hashes really do run in parallel with the loop.
Instead of
Hashing on the loop, or without a limit.
Why
One hash takes tens of milliseconds of CPU. On the loop, every sign-in would freeze that replica for that long. Without a limit, a burst of sign-ins would exhaust memory: the library's default profile uses 64 MiB per hash, so 100 sign-ins at once would need over 6 GB. With the semaphore, extra sign-ins wait their turn instead.
D15

A connection budget, and timeouts on every wait

your call
Choice
Async SQLAlchemy on asyncpg. Each replica has a pool of 10 connections plus 5 overflow, a 5-second wait for a free one, and pool_pre_ping. Postgres runs with statement_timeout 5 s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 10 s. Each request gets its own AsyncSession and one transaction, committed on success and rolled back on any exception. Sessions are never shared between concurrent coroutines, because an AsyncSession isn't safe for that.
Budget
Total connections = replicas × 15, kept under 80% of Postgres's 100. That's 30 in round 1 and 45 in round 2. Round 3 adds autoscaling, so it puts the PgBouncer built into Azure's Postgres in front.
Why
Requests are short, so 15 connections serve many concurrent users. When load exceeds that, requests wait up to 5 seconds and then get a clear 503, rather than an unbounded queue taking down the database.
Many requests touching the same rows

Races and consistency

Tasks are private, so two different users never contend for the same row. The races that remain come from one user (two tabs, fast drags, a double-click) and from users signing up with the same email. Every guard lives in Postgres, because a lock inside one Python process means nothing to the other replica.

D16

Order changes are serialized per user, in Postgres

your call
Choice
Creating a task and moving one each start their transaction with pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text, 0)), then read the neighbours, compute the rank and write. A unique index on (owner_id, rank) backs it up. Edits and deletes don't take the lock, since they never change ranks.
Isolation
Postgres's default, READ COMMITTED, and that's deliberate. Each statement reads a fresh snapshot, so the neighbour read after the lock is granted sees the other move's commit. Under REPEATABLE READ the snapshot would be taken at the lock statement, before that commit, and both moves would compute the same rank.
Instead of
An asyncio.Lock, which only covers one process. SERIALIZABLE everywhere, which needs retry loops on every write. A version check on the whole list.
Why
The lock is the narrowest correct one: one user's ordering writes queue for a few milliseconds, and nothing else waits.
D17

Edits can't silently overwrite each other

your call
Choice
Each task has an integer version. Responses carry it as an ETag. PATCH with If-Match updates only when the version still matches (UPDATE … WHERE id = :id AND owner_id = :me AND version = :v) and answers 412 when it doesn't. The detail screen always sends If-Match; on a 412 it shows the newer version and offers to apply the change again. PATCH changes only the fields sent.
Instead of
Last write wins, which is what most To Do apps do.
Why
Editing the same task in two tabs is the one lost-update case this app has. One conditional UPDATE closes it without locks. If-Match stays optional, so scripted clients still work.
RaceGuardTest that proves it
Two sign-ups with one emailUnique index on email; the insert's IntegrityError becomes 409. Never check-then-insert.Integration: 20 concurrent sign-ups, exactly one 201 and nineteen 409s
Moves and creates in one list at oncePer-user advisory lock, unique (owner_id, rank)Integration: 50 concurrent moves; afterwards the ranks are unique and the list holds the same tasks. Live: the same through both replicas
Two tabs edit one taskversion, If-Match, 412Integration: two PATCHes on the same version, one 200 and one 412
Edit or toggle after deleteOwner-scoped UPDATE affects 0 rows → 404Component: a 404 on a mutation removes the row and says why
A late search response overwrites a newer oneResults cached per search term; superseded requests aborted with AbortSignalHook test: MSW delays the response for "ab" past the one for "abc", and "abc" stays on screen
A refetch lands on top of an optimistic reordercancelQueries before the optimistic write; reorder mutations share one scope, so they run in orderComponent: three quick moves end in the order the user made
Something blocks the event loopAsync-only handlers, hashing off the loop (D13, D14)Backend fixture: asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold; a test fails if any callback blocks longer
Load beyond the limitsRequest, connection and hash limits; 503 with the envelope (D13 to D15)Load test (D18): no 5xx at target load, p95 within budget
D18

A load test before submission

your call
Choice
k6, run from its official container as a compose profile (docker compose --profile load run k6), so nothing needs installing. 200 virtual users, each with its own account, ramp up over 1 minute and hold for 3. Each one loops: list, search, create, toggle, move, edit, delete, with 1 second of think time. After the run, a check script confirms every user's list has unique ranks and the expected number of tasks.
Pass
Under 0.1% failed requests and no 5xx. p95 latency under 250 ms for reads and under 400 ms for writes; under 1.5 s for sign-in, which queues on purpose (D14). Results are saved with the machine's specs and quoted in the README.
Instead of
Locust, which is Python and fits the backend, but lacks k6's built-in pass/fail thresholds.
Why
It shows the limits in D13 to D16 working under real concurrency, and gives reviewers a script they can rerun at their own scale.

How we explain it in the deep-dive

  • One request, end to end: every log line carries request_id, user_id, duration_ms and the replica that served it, so a single slow or failed request can be followed across both replicas.
  • Each race has a test with the race in its name, from the table above, and each one fails if its guard is removed.
  • The load test summary (throughput, p95 per endpoint, error rate, the consistency check) goes in the README next to this section's diagrams.
Contract

+      <figcaption>Everything the loop hands off has a limit: 200 requests in progress per replica, 15 database connections, 4 hashes at a time. When a limit is reached, requests wait for a bounded time; past that wait the client gets a 503 with the error envelope, never a hung connection.</figcaption>

+

One uvicorn process per container, every handler async

your call

+
Choice
uvicorn[standard] (uvloop, httptools) with one worker per container; more capacity means more replicas. Every route is async def and uses only async libraries. --limit-concurrency 200 answers 503 past 200 in-flight requests. --timeout-graceful-shutdown 20 lets in-flight requests finish on SIGTERM, then the lifespan closes the pool. Nginx keeps connections to the API open and caps request bodies at 64 KB.

+
Instead of
Gunicorn or uvicorn managing several worker processes inside one container. Or plain def handlers, which FastAPI runs on a thread pool capped at 40 threads by default.

+          <dt>Why</dt><dd>One process per container lets Docker and Kubernetes restart it, count it and scale it, and each pod's memory and CPU stay predictable. Async-only handlers mean the loop is the only scheduler to reason about.</dd>

+

Password hashing runs off the loop, at most four at a time

your call

+
Choice
argon2id with OWASP's parameters (19 MiB memory, 2 passes, 1 lane), run through asyncio.to_thread behind an asyncio.Semaphore(4) per process. argon2-cffi releases the GIL while it hashes, so the hashes really do run in parallel with the loop.
+          <dt>Instead of</dt><dd>Hashing on the loop, or without a limit.</dd>

+          <dt>Why</dt><dd>One hash takes tens of milliseconds of CPU. On the loop, every sign-in would freeze that replica for that long. Without a limit, a burst of sign-ins would exhaust memory: the library's default profile uses 64 MiB per hash, so 100 sign-ins at once would need over 6 GB. With the semaphore, extra sign-ins wait their turn instead.</dd>

+

A connection budget, and timeouts on every wait

your call

+
Choice
Async SQLAlchemy on asyncpg. Each replica has a pool of 10 connections plus 5 overflow, a 5-second wait for a free one, and pool_pre_ping. Postgres runs with statement_timeout 5 s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 10 s. Each request gets its own AsyncSession and one transaction, committed on success and rolled back on any exception. Sessions are never shared between concurrent coroutines, because an AsyncSession isn't safe for that.

+          <dt>Budget</dt><dd>Total connections = replicas × 15, kept under 80% of Postgres's 100. That's 30 in round 1 and 45 in round 2. Round 3 adds autoscaling, so it puts the PgBouncer built into Azure's Postgres in front.</dd>

+          <dt>Why</dt><dd>Requests are short, so 15 connections serve many concurrent users. When load exceeds that, requests wait up to 5 seconds and then get a clear 503, rather than an unbounded queue taking down the database.</dd>
+ Many requests touching the same rows

+

Tasks are private, so two different users never contend for the same row. The races that remain come from one user (two tabs, fast drags, a double-click) and from users signing up with the same email. Every guard lives in Postgres, because a lock inside one Python process means nothing to the other replica.

+        <svg viewBox="0 0 900 400" role="img" aria-label="Two moves for the same user arrive at different replicas. api-1 takes the per-user lock first, reads neighbours a0 and a1, writes X as a0V and commits. api-2 waits for the lock, then reads the new neighbours a0 and a0V and writes Y as a0F. your call

+
Choice
Creating a task and moving one each start their transaction with pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text, 0)), then read the neighbours, compute the rank and write. A unique index on (owner_id, rank) backs it up. Edits and deletes don't take the lock, since they never change ranks.

Each statement reads a fresh snapshot, so the neighbour read after the lock is granted sees the other move's commit. Under REPEATABLE READ the snapshot would be taken at the lock statement, before that commit, and both moves would compute the same rank.</dd>

your call

+
Choice

+

+ Two tabs edit one taskversion, If-Match, 412Integration: two PATCHes on the same version, one 200 and one 412
+ Edit or toggle after deleteOwner-scoped UPDATE affects 0 rows → 404Component: a 404 on a mutation removes the row and says why

+ A late search response overwrites a newer oneResults cached per search term; superseded requests aborted with AbortSignalHook test: MSW delays the response for "ab" past the one for "abc", and "abc" stays on screen

+ A refetch lands on top of an optimistic reordercancelQueries before the optimistic write; reorder mutations share one scope, so they run in orderComponent: three quick moves end in the order the user made

+ Something blocks the event loopAsync-only handlers, hashing off the loop (D13, D14)Backend fixture: asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold; a test fails if any callback blocks longer
+ Load beyond the limitsRequest, connection and hash limits; 503 with the envelope (D13 to D15)Load test (D18): no 5xx at target load, p95 within budget

+

A load test before submission

your call

+
Choice
k6, run from its official container as a compose profile (docker compose --profile load run k6), so nothing needs installing. 200 virtual users, each with its own account, ramp up over 1 minute and hold for 3. Each one loops: list, search, create, toggle, move, edit, delete, with 1 second of think time. After the run, a check script confirms every user's list has unique ranks and the expected number of tasks.

+          <dt>Pass</dt><dd>Under 0.1% failed requests and no 5xx. p95 latency under 250 ms for reads and under 400 ms for writes; under 1.5 s for sign-in, which queues on purpose (D14). Results are saved with the machine's specs and quoted in the README.</dd>
+          <dt>Instead of</dt><dd>Locust, which is Python and fits the backend, but lacks k6's built-in pass/fail thresholds.</dd>
+          <dt>Why</dt><dd>It shows the limits in D13 to D16 working under real concurrency, and gives reviewers a script they can rerun at their own scale.</dd>

+

How we explain it in the deep-dive

+
  • One request, end to end: every log line carries request_id, user_id, duration_ms and the replica that served it, so a single slow or failed request can be followed across both replicas.

+
  • Each race has a test with the race in its name, from the table above, and each one fails if its guard is removed.

+
  • The load test summary (throughput, p95 per endpoint, error rate, the consistency check) goes in the README next to this section's diagrams.

.claude/rules/deployment.md:26:- Every backend pod has a liveness probe (`/healthz`, process up) and a readiness probe (`/readyz`, database reachable). Requests and limits are set. Containers run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem where the runtime allows. docs/specs/round-1.html:291:
Choice
API logs are JSON lines on stdout. Each request gets one access line (request_id, user_id, method, route, status, duration_ms), plus a startup "ready" line and every caught error with context. X-Request-ID is accepted from the caller or created, and echoed back. /healthz and /readyz are the probes. In the SPA: console.info when it boots, and console.error from the error boundary and the global query error handler.
docs/specs/round-1.html:625:
Why
No standard path exists: the IETF's health-check format never went past a draft. The trailing z is Google's convention for keeping probe paths clear of app routes. Kubernetes deprecated /healthz for its own API server in v1.16 in favour of separate /livez and /readyz, and we follow that split. Keeping them separate matters: if liveness checked the database, a short database outage would make Kubernetes restart every API pod at once, turning a blip into an outage. Readiness only takes a pod out of rotation.

input.content:
# Future work

Ideas we chose not to build in rounds 1 to 3, and why each is worth doing. The README's "given more time" section draws from this list.

## Identity
- **Sign-in with Microsoft, Google or Apple.** OpenID Connect through the provider each client already uses (Microsoft Entra ID for a Microsoft shop, Google or Apple for consumers). Email and password stay as the fallback.
- **Refresh-token rotation and revocation.** Short-lived access tokens, a rotating refresh token, and a deny list, so a stolen or signed-out session can be ended before it expires.
- **Email verification and password reset.** Both need an outbound email service.

## AI features (after everything else works)
- **Create and update tasks by describing them.** The user types or speaks ("move the dentist to Friday and add a note to bring the form") and the app turns that into task creates and updates. The model's output is untrusted: it is parsed into the same typed models the API already validates, and the user confirms the changes before they are applied.
- **An AI summary home page.** A home screen that summarises what is due, overdue and done, streamed to the client, possibly built on the AG-UI protocol for agent-to-UI events.

## Data and scale
- **Rank rebalancing.** A background job that rewrites long ranks in a list to short ones, run when a rank passes a length limit.
- **Paging for long lists.** A cursor on `GET /api/v1/tasks`; the `{"items": [...]}` envelope already leaves room for it.
- **Sign-in rate limiting.** It needs a store shared by every replica (Redis, or the ingress), so it waits for round 2 or 3.

I've updated the spec with your feedback and decisions and republished it to the same link: **https://claude.ai/artifact/3dkwrN9PYso4kEmYhZSUG1**. Nothing new is committed; the changes sit in the working tree on `docs/round-1-spec` until your final review.

## What changed in the spec
- **Your seven decisions are locked,** with your notes. The two API copies stay in round 1, since your decision 6 withdrew feedback point 3.
- **New "Async and concurrency" section,** with a diagram of what happens inside one API copy. Its core idea: one uvicorn process runs one event loop for all requests, so anything slow on that loop stalls everyone using that copy. Three decisions follow:
  - **D13:** one uvicorn process per container, every handler async, at most 200 requests in progress per copy (then a clear 503), and a clean shutdown that finishes in-flight requests.
  - **D14:** password hashing runs off the loop, at most 4 at a time per copy. This one matters most: the hashing library's default uses 64 MiB per hash, so 100 sign-ins at once would need over 6 GB.
  - **D15:** a budget of 15 database connections per copy, kept under Postgres's limit, plus timeouts on every wait.
- **New "Races and consistency" section,** with a step-by-step diagram of two moves arriving at different API copies at once:
  - **D16:** reorder writes for one user go one at a time, using a lock held in Postgres. A lock inside Python wouldn't cover the other copy. It also depends on Postgres's default isolation level: a stricter level would make both moves compute the same position.
  - **D17:** two tabs editing the same task can't silently overwrite each other; the stale edit gets a 412.
  - **A table of 8 race cases,** each with its guard and the test that proves it.
  - **D18:** a load test with k6, run from its container: 200 users, response-time targets, and a check afterwards that every user's data is intact.
  - **How to explain each of these in the deep-dive.**
- **D19 health checks:** `/livez` and `/readyz`. There's no official standard (the proposed IETF format never got past a draft), and Kubernetes itself deprecated `/healthz` in favour of this split. The liveness check deliberately doesn't touch the database; otherwise a short database outage would restart every API copy at once.
- **Order of work, D20 design first:** your reviewers approve the actual screen code that ships, not a separate drawing. Screens are written once as React views that receive their data as props. A second build renders every screen in every state with sample data, and that build is published as the design artifact. Later the frontend PR connects the same views to real data, so nothing is built twice.

Before updating anything, on D17: **yes, your understanding is right.**

  - **If-Match/412** stays as the guarantee underneath.

])
edit(".claude/rules/python.md", [
("## Async and boot\n- asyncio throughout. Do not block the event loop: no sync database driver, no blocking hashing on the loop.\n",
 "## Async and boot\n- asyncio throughout. Every route is `async def`; a plain `def` route would run on FastAPI's thread pool. Do not block the event loop: no sync database driver, no sync HTTP client, no blocking file I/O on the request path.\n- CPU-heavy work runs through `asyncio.to_thread` behind a semaphore that caps it per process. Password hashing (argon2id, OWASP parameters) is capped at 4 at a time.\n- One `AsyncSession` and one transaction per request, from a dependency; commit on success, roll back on any exception. Never share a session between concurrent coroutines; a `TaskGroup` that touches the database gives each task its own session.\n- Logging goes through a `QueueHandler` so a slow stdout never blocks the loop.\n"),
])
edit(".claude/rules/database.md", [
("- Every query against `tasks` filters on the owner.",
 "- Transactions run at READ COMMITTED, Postgres's default. Do not raise it: the ordering lock below depends on each statement reading a fresh snapshot.\n- Creating or moving a task takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text, 0))` as the first statement of its transaction, then reads the neighbours. A unique index on `(owner_id, rank)` backs it up. Edits and deletes do not take the lock.\n- `rank` is `text COLLATE \"C\"` so Postgres sorts it byte by byte, like Python. Edits check `version` in the `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` and bump it.\n- Unique facts are enforced by unique indexes, and the insert's `IntegrityError` becomes 409. Never check-then-insert.\n- Pool: 10 connections plus 5 overflow per process, 5 s wait, `pool_pre_ping`; `statement_timeout` 5 s and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` 10 s on every connection.\n- Every query against `tasks` filters on the owner."),
])
print("rules updated")
PYEOF

14	
15	Do not start a stage before the previous one is proven and the human says go.
16	
17	## The human reviews every deployment artifact
18	- Dockerfiles, compose files, Kubernetes manifests, overlays and workflows are shown to the human and approved before they are applied or merged. Show the file and say what it will create or change.
19	- The agent never applies anything to AKS or any shared cloud resource. It prepares the change and the exact command; the human runs it (`CONTRIBUTING.md` § 11). `kubectl apply`, `kubectl delete`, `helm` and `az` always ask, even against k3d.
20	
21	## Built for more than one replica
22	- One uvicorn process per container; scale with replicas, never with in-container workers.
23	- The backend is stateless: auth is a signed token checked on every request, with no in-memory sessions or caches that requests write to. Any replica can serve any request.
24	- One set of manifests (Kustomize base) with one overlay per target (`k3d`, `aks`). No copy-pasted manifests per environment.
25	- Images are tagged with the git sha, never `latest`, and the same image moves from one stage to the next.
26	- Migrations run once per release as a Job before the backend rolls out, never from every pod at startup.
27	- Every backend pod has a liveness probe (`/livez`, process up, checks no dependencies) and a readiness probe (`/readyz`, database reachable, fails once shutdown starts). Neither is routed by nginx or the ingress. Requests and limits are set. Containers run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem where the runtime allows.
28	- Config comes from env vars through ConfigMaps; secrets come from Kubernetes Secrets the human creates. Neither is ever committed.

8	# Database
9	
10	- Schema changes go through a new alembic migration, numbered after the last one. Never edit a migration that has been applied anywhere. Never change the database by hand.
11	- Run migrations with `uv run alembic upgrade head` from `backend/`. Deployed environments run them as a one-shot step (a Kubernetes Job or init step) before the new pods take traffic, never from app startup, because several replicas would race.
12	- Every migration has a working `downgrade`. CI runs upgrade, downgrade and upgrade again.
13	- Every query is parameterized through SQLAlchemy. No string-built SQL. Index every column used in WHERE, JOIN or ORDER BY, starting with `tasks(owner_id, position)`.
14	- Transactions run at READ COMMITTED, Postgres's default. Do not raise it: the ordering lock below depends on each statement reading a fresh snapshot.
15	- Creating or moving a task takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text, 0))` as the first statement of its transaction, then reads the neighbours. A unique index on `(owner_id, rank)` backs it up. Edits and deletes do not take the lock.
16	- `rank` is `text COLLATE "C"` so Postgres sorts it byte by byte, like Python. Edits check `version` in the `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` and bump it.
17	- Unique facts are enforced by unique indexes, and the insert's `IntegrityError` becomes 409. Never check-then-insert.
18	- Pool: 10 connections plus 5 overflow per process, 5 s wait, `pool_pre_ping`; `statement_timeout` 5 s and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` 10 s on every connection.
19	- Every query against `tasks` filters on the owner. A query without the owner filter is a bug, even in an admin path.
20	- Writes that must stay consistent (reorder, delete with a position gap) run in one transaction.

attachment.snippet:
21	- Build the app in a factory (`create_app(settings)`) so tests build their own app with their own settings.
22	
23	## Failure handling and logging
24	- On a validation error at a boundary: log at WARNING with the function name, the error, and a sanitized snippet, then take the documented fail-soft path. Never silent.
25	- `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`. No `print`. The root logger is configured once, in the app factory, before any request is served.
26	- WARNING and ERROR lines say where (`module.function`), why, and what happens next, with ids as key=value. Never log secrets.
27	
28	## Async and boot
29	- asyncio throughout. Every route is `async def`; a plain `def` route would run on FastAPI's thread pool. Do not block the event loop: no sync database driver, no sync HTTP client, no blocking file I/O on the request path.
30	- CPU-heavy work runs through `asyncio.to_thread` behind a semaphore that caps it per process. Password hashing (argon2id, OWASP parameters) is capped at 4 at a time.
31	- One `AsyncSession` and one transaction per request, from a dependency; commit on success, roll back on any exception. Never share a session between concurrent coroutines; a `TaskGroup` that touches the database gives each task its own session.
32	- Logging goes through a `QueueHandler` so a slow stdout never blocks the loop.
33	- Never add a network call at import time; put it in the lifespan. A database the app cannot reach makes `/readyz` fail, not the import.

input.prompt:
You are the planning engineer on `todo-app`, a full-stack To Do list built for an engineering challenge that will be reviewed line by line in a live deep-dive. Your job: write the detailed coding plan for round 1 (the app running in containers). You write a plan document, not code.

## Read first, in full
- `TASK.md` (the challenge brief), `docs/kickoff.md` (requirements, the lead's feedback verbatim, locked decisions), `CLAUDE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, every file in `.claude/rules/`.
- `docs/specs/round-1.html`: the signed-off spec, decisions D1 to D20. It is the source of truth. Read the HTML text closely, including the tables and the figure captions.
- `FUTURE.md` (what is out of scope).

## Goal
Produce `docs/plans/round-1.md`: a plan precise enough that an engineer could build round 1 from it without making a design decision the spec didn't already make, and that the lead can skim in tables. Every spec decision (D1 to D20) must be traceable to where the plan implements it.

## Scope: what the plan must contain
1. **Traceability table:** spec id to plan section(s).
2. **Repo layout:** every backend module and file with one line on what it owns (functional core in `backend/app/domain/`, thin routers, services, repositories, db models, settings, app factory, middleware). Frontend data layer and containers (see the shared contract below). `e2e/` (live API tests, Playwright), `load/` (k6), compose and Docker files.
3. **Backend detail:**
   - Settings: every env var, its type, default, and whether it's required. Then the exact lines for `.env.example`. The human creates that file; agents never write it.
   - App factory, lifespan (pool create and dispose), middleware (request id, access log, `X-Served-By`, `Origin` check on writes giving 403), exception handlers (422 to 400, domain errors, one error envelope).
   - SQLAlchemy models. The first alembic migration as a DDL outline: extensions `citext` and `pg_trgm`, tables, `rank text COLLATE "C"`, `version`, checks, unique `(owner_id, rank)`, trigram GIN index, unique email.
   - Pydantic request and response models: camelCase on the wire via `alias_generator=to_camel`.
   - Domain core function signatures with their contracts. `rank_between` gets its algorithm spelled out (base-62 midpoint keys; show the worked example `rank_between("a0","a1") == "a0V"` and `rank_between("a0","a0V") == "a0F"`). Also `search_pattern`, which escapes `%`, `_` and `\`, and `apply_patch`.
   - Repositories and services, with transaction boundaries and the advisory lock placement (D16). The conditional `UPDATE` with version (D17).
   - Auth: JWT claims, lifetime and cookie attributes. argon2id with OWASP parameters behind `to_thread` and `Semaphore(4)` (D14).
   - Concurrency config: uvicorn flags (D13), pool and timeouts (D15). `/livez` and `/readyz` (D19). JSON logging through `QueueHandler` (D11).
4. **Frontend data layer:**
   - The fetch wrapper and `ApiError`, and the query key factory.
   - Query and mutation hooks: optimistic toggle, reorder and delete with rollback; reorder mutations share one `scope`; `cancelQueries` before optimistic writes; `AbortSignal` for search; 250 ms debounce.
   - `refetchOnWindowFocus`, and the "Changed elsewhere" detection for D17: a cached version newer than the draft's base version.
   - Global 401 handling, the auth context and route guard, router config, the error boundary, and `console.info`/`console.error` usage.
   - One container per route that wires a view to these hooks.
5. **Containers (round 1):**
   - Backend Dockerfile: multi-stage with uv, non-root.
   - Frontend Dockerfile: build stage, then an unprivileged nginx.
   - `nginx.conf`: SPA fallback, `/api/` proxied to an upstream with keepalive, 64 KB body limit, security headers including a CSP, probes not routed.
   - `docker-compose.yml`: `db`, a one-shot `migrate` that must succeed before `api` starts, `api` with 2 replicas, `web` on 8080 as the only published port, and a `k6` service under a `load` profile. Healthchecks for each.
6. **Test plan:** for each of the five layers plus load, list the test files and the test names (behaviour-named).
   - Every race in the spec's race table gets a named test. Say how it fires concurrent requests (`asyncio.TaskGroup`, separate connections) and how we show it fails without its guard.
   - The asyncio debug-mode slow-callback fixture.
   - Database fixture strategy: the race tests need real commits across connections, so say how test isolation works, for example a dedicated test database with truncation between tests.
   - Hypothesis properties for `rank_between`, and the Postgres-vs-Python sort agreement test.
   - The k6 script outline, its budgets, and the stepped capacity run (D18).
   - Coverage configuration (90/85).
7. **CI:** the jobs and their steps (hygiene plus hook tests exist already; add backend with a Postgres service container, frontend, and e2e with compose).
8. **Delivery sequence:** the PRs in order and, inside each, the commit sequence in test-first order: which test goes red, then what makes it green. Every commit must be green.
   - Mark the checkpoints where the lead must be present: the race tests (watch them fail without the guard, then pass) and the load test (review scripts and budgets first, then walk through the results).
   - Mark the review gates.
   - Per PR, give the size as bounded work (files, migrations, PR rounds), never human hours or days (see the workspace's time-estimation rule). Name external waits separately.
9. **Risks and open questions.** Anything the spec doesn't settle goes here as a question with your recommendation. Never decide silently.

## Shared contract with the design engineer (working in parallel on the frontend views)
Another agent is building the design system and every screen as **presentational views** on branch `feature/web-design-system`. Plan around these names exactly:
- Tokens: `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css` (Tailwind 4 `@theme`).
- Primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui/`. App shell: `frontend/src/components/app-shell.tsx` (`AppShell`).
- Views, props in and JSX out, no fetching and no TanStack Query inside: `frontend/src/views/sign-in-view.tsx` (`SignInView`), `sign-up-view.tsx` (`SignUpView`), `task-list-view.tsx` (`TaskListView`), `task-detail-view.tsx` (`TaskDetailView`), `not-found-view.tsx` (`NotFoundView`). The design engineer defines their prop interfaces. Your plan's containers pass data and callbacks into them; describe the props each container must supply from the spec's states (loading, empty, error, ready, saving, field errors, changed elsewhere, reorder disabled while searching). Mark the frontend wiring section as "to reconcile with the views' final props".
- Zod schemas owned by the design branch: `frontend/src/lib/schema/task.ts` (`taskSchema`, `Task`, `taskListSchema`) and `frontend/src/lib/schema/auth.ts` (`credentialsSchema`, `userSchema`, `User`). The fields follow spec D8 plus `id`, `rank`, `version`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, all camelCase.
- Shared fixtures: `frontend/src/test/fixtures.ts`, used by both the component tests and the design gallery.
- The frontend toolchain (Vite, React 19, TS strict, Tailwind 4, ESLint, Prettier, Vitest, RTL, npm) is scaffolded by the design branch. Your plan covers what is added on top of it: the router, TanStack Query, MSW, the fetch wrapper, the containers and Playwright.

## Constraints
- Work in your worktree. First create and switch to branch `docs/round-1-plan`.
- Write only `docs/plans/round-1.md`. Do not edit the spec, the rules, CLAUDE.md or code. If something in them looks wrong, list it under open questions.
- Never read or write `.env` files, `.env.example` or key material; the hooks block it. Put the `.env.example` lines in the plan.
- Code in the plan is limited to signatures, short DDL and config fragments, and pseudo-steps; no implementations. Follow the repo's writing style: plain English, short sentences, tables where they help.
- Check facts you rely on against official docs when unsure (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy async, asyncpg, uvicorn flags, TanStack Query v5, k6), and cite the doc in the plan when a choice depends on it.
- When done: run `python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py`, then commit the plan as one commit: `docs(plan): add the round 1 coding plan` with a why-focused body and the trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Do not push and do not open a PR.

## Report back (your final message)
- **Branch and commit:** the branch name and the commit sha.
- **Shape:** a 10-line summary of the plan's shape.
- **Decisions you made** that the spec didn't spell out, each with a reason.
- **Open questions,** each with your recommendation.
- **Spec or rule contradictions** you found, if any.

input.description: Build design system and screens
input.prompt:
You are the design engineer on `todo-app`, a full-stack To Do list built for an engineering challenge that will be reviewed line by line in a live deep-dive. Your job: build the frontend's design system and every screen as **real, shippable React components**, rendered in a design gallery that is published as the design artifact the lead reviews. What the lead approves is the code that ships, so nothing gets built twice.

## Read first, in full
- `TASK.md`, `docs/kickoff.md` (especially the lead's feedback), `CLAUDE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and every file in `.claude/rules/`. `typescript.md`, `react.md`, `testing.md` and `coding-standards.md` bind you.
- `docs/specs/round-1.html`: the signed-off spec. The sections that drive your work are Screens, D17 (the "Changed elsewhere" notice), D20 (how this design work is built), D6 (reordering, off while searching), D7 (search), D8 (fields) and D3/D4 (accounts).

## Design direction (from the lead, verbatim)
"stellar look and premium feel + vintage colors + 0 redundancy"

How to read that:
- **Vintage colours:** draw them from one specific, real vintage source suited to a task list, not a generic "retro" look. Examples: library card catalogues and index cards, a ledger, mid-century railway timetables, Penguin paperback covers, enamel signage. Name your source and derive every colour from it.
- **Avoid the generic AI looks:** warm cream background with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green pop; purple-to-blue gradients; Inter or Space Grotesk; emoji as icons; rounded-lg and shadow on everything.
- **Premium feel:** precise typographic hierarchy with a characterful display face used with restraint and a quiet, highly legible body face. Generous, consistent spacing on a scale. Depth that is subtle and used by role. Restrained motion that respects `prefers-reduced-motion`. Careful focus states. Both light and dark themes designed with equal care, each meeting WCAG AA contrast.
- **Zero redundancy:**
  - **Tokens:** every colour, size, radius, shadow and duration is a token in one file.
  - **Composition:** components are composed from primitives.
  - **Shared fixtures:** the gallery and the component tests use the same fixtures.
  - **One code path:** no screen is drawn any other way than through the real view component.

## Shared contract (another agent is writing the coding plan in parallel and relies on these exact names)
- Tokens: `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css`, using Tailwind 4 `@theme` variables. The light palette is defined on `:root`; dark comes from `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])`, and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, so it works both in the app and in the artifact viewer, which sets `data-theme`.
- Primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui/` (for example button, text field, checkbox, search box, task row, sortable list, empty state, inline confirm, notice or banner, skeleton). Choose the set the screens need, nothing speculative. App shell: `frontend/src/components/app-shell.tsx` (`AppShell`).
- Views: props in, JSX out. No data fetching, no TanStack Query, no router hooks inside a view; callbacks out. Files:
  - `frontend/src/views/sign-in-view.tsx` (`SignInView`)
  - `sign-up-view.tsx` (`SignUpView`)
  - `task-list-view.tsx` (`TaskListView`)
  - `task-detail-view.tsx` (`TaskDetailView`)
  - `not-found-view.tsx` (`NotFoundView`)

  Export each view's props interface. Design the props so a container can wire TanStack Query to them later without the view changing. Local UI state (a draft form value, an open confirm) may live in the view with `useState`. Server data never does.
- Every state the spec implies must be expressible through props and shown in the gallery:
  - Task list: loading, empty, error, ready with completed and open tasks and a due date, searching with results, searching with no results, reorder disabled while searching, a pending create.
  - Task detail: viewing and editing, saving, field errors, "Changed elsewhere" (newer version under an unsaved draft), the delete confirm, not found.
  - Sign in and sign up: idle, submitting, field errors, wrong credentials (401), email taken (409).
- Reordering uses dnd-kit with pointer, touch and keyboard sensors. The view emits `onMove(taskId, afterId | null)`.
- Zod schemas: `frontend/src/lib/schema/task.ts` (`taskSchema`, `Task`, `taskListSchema`) and `frontend/src/lib/schema/auth.ts` (`credentialsSchema`, `userSchema`, `User`). Fields follow spec D8 plus `id`, `rank`, `version`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, camelCase. Types come from `z.infer`. Title is 1 to 200 characters, notes at most 5,000, password 12 to 128. Forms validate with these same schemas.
- Fixtures: `frontend/src/test/fixtures.ts`, realistic task content, shared by tests and the gallery.
- Design gallery: a second Vite entry at `frontend/design/` (`index.html` and `main.tsx`). It renders a token sheet (colour swatches with names and contrast ratios, the type scale, spacing, radii, motion) and then every view in every state, each at phone width (390 px) and desktop width (1280 px) frames. `npm run design:build` produces one self-contained HTML file at `frontend/design/dist/artifact.html`:
  - **Inlined:** all JS, CSS and fonts. Self-host fonts with `@fontsource` packages, so the app and the gallery share them, and inline them in the design build only.
  - **No wrapper tags:** no `<!doctype>`, `<html>`, `<head>` or `<body>`. The artifact host wraps the file itself, so strip them in a small post-build step, and put a `<title>` near the top.
  - **No network calls,** and nothing relying on browser storage.
  - **Under 16 MB.**

## Frontend scaffold (yours to create, since the views need it)
- **Toolchain:** Node 24 and npm (commit `package-lock.json`), Vite, React 19, TypeScript strict (also `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`), Tailwind 4 via `@tailwindcss/vite`.
- **ESLint** (flat config):
  - `typescript-eslint` strict and type-checked rule sets.
  - `react-hooks` with `rules-of-hooks` and `exhaustive-deps` as errors.
  - `no-console` as an error, allowing only info, warn and error.
- **Prettier.**
- **Testing:** Vitest with jsdom, React Testing Library, user-event and jest-dom. The coverage threshold is 85% lines and branches in `vitest.config.ts`.
- **Scripts:** `dev`, `build`, `check` (ESLint + `prettier --check` + `tsc --noEmit`), `test` (Vitest with coverage), `design:build`.
- **`frontend/CLAUDE.md`:** short, covering commands, layout and gotchas. The root `CLAUDE.md` already points to it.
- **CI:** add a `frontend` job to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (npm ci, check, test, build).
Don't add the router, TanStack Query, MSW or a fetch wrapper; those come with the data layer later.

## Engineering rules that bind you
- **Test first:** red, then green, inside your session. Every commit is green: `npm run check && npm run test && npm run build` all pass before each commit.
  - Test behaviour a user can see: roles, names, text, callbacks fired with the right arguments. Never test class names.
  - Each view gets tests for its states, and interactive primitives get tests for their interactions.
  - No redundant tests: a primitive's behaviour is tested once on the primitive, not again through every view.
- **Functional, declarative style:** pure helpers (for example date formatting, due-date status) are exported and unit-tested, with no mutation (use `toSorted` and friends).
- **JSDoc** on every export. Kebab-case files. Named exports. Accessible markup: labels, real buttons, visible focus, 44 px touch targets, responsive from 320 px.
- **Visual QA is mandatory:**
  - Use Playwright (as a dev dependency; run `npx playwright install chromium`) to screenshot the built gallery at 390 px and 1280 px wide, in both light and dark (set `data-theme`).
  - Look at the screenshots with your Read tool and fix what you see: alignment, contrast, spacing rhythm, overflow, anything that isn't premium.
  - Save the final screenshots under `frontend/design/screenshots/` and commit them, so the lead can see them in the PR.

## Constraints
- Work in your worktree. First create and switch to branch `feature/web-design-system`.
- Touch only `frontend/`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the frontend job) and nothing else. Never read or write `.env` files.
- Conventional commits (`feat(web): ...`, `chore(web): ...`, `test(web): ...`) with why-focused bodies, one logical change each, each ending with the trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Do not push and do not open a PR.

## Work in two phases. Stop after phase 1.
**Phase 1, the direction checkpoint:**
1. The scaffold.
2. The tokens, with a short written rationale: the vintage source, the palette with names and roles, the type pairing, the spacing and radius scale.
3. The primitives that `TaskListView` needs.
4. `TaskListView` in all its states.
5. The gallery showing the token sheet plus `TaskListView`.
6. Screenshots at both widths and in both themes.

All committed and green. Then STOP and end your turn with the phase 1 report below. The tech lead will review the direction and either send corrections or tell you to continue.

**Phase 2, only after the go-ahead:**
1. The remaining views with all their states, plus `AppShell`.
2. The full gallery and the final screenshots.
3. `frontend/CLAUDE.md` and the CI job.
4. A final self-review against this brief.

## Report format (end of each phase)
- **Branch and commits:** the branch name and the commit shas with their subjects.
- **Tests:** the exact pass counts and coverage numbers from your last `npm run test`.
- **Direction:** the design direction in 5 lines (source, palette, type, feel).
- **Screenshots:** their paths.
- **Decisions:** any you made that the brief didn't settle, with reasons.
- **Weaknesses:** anything you're unhappy with, or would do with more time.

Your job: build the frontend's design system and every screen as **real, shippable React components**, rendered in a design gallery that is published as the design artifact the lead reviews. What the lead approves is the code that ships, so nothing gets built twice.

## Read first, in full
- `TASK.md`, `docs/kickoff.md` (especially the lead's feedback), `CLAUDE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and every file in `.claude/rules/`. `typescript.md`, `react.md`, `testing.md` and `coding-standards.md` bind you.
- `docs/specs/round-1.html`: the signed-off spec. The sections that drive your work are Screens, D17 (the "Changed elsewhere" notice), D20 (how this design work is built), D6 (reordering, off while searching), D7 (search), D8 (fields) and D3/D4 (accounts).

## Design direction (from the lead, verbatim)
"stellar look and premium feel + vintage colors + 0 redundancy"

How to read that:
- **Vintage colours:** draw them from one specific, real vintage source suited to a task list, not a generic "retro" look. Examples: library card catalogues and index cards, a ledger, mid-century railway timetables, Penguin paperback covers, enamel signage. Name your source and derive every colour from it.
- **Avoid the generic AI looks:** warm cream background with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green pop; purple-to-blue gradients; Inter or Space Grotesk; emoji as icons; rounded-lg and shadow on everything.
- **Premium feel:** precise typographic hierarchy with a characterful display face used with restraint and a quiet, highly legible body face. Generous, consistent spacing on a scale. Depth that is subtle and used by role. Restrained motion that respects `prefers-reduced-motion`. Careful focus states. Both light and dark themes designed with equal care, each meeting WCAG AA contrast.
- **Zero redundancy:**
  - **Tokens:** every colour, size, radius, shadow and duration is a token in one file.
  - **Composition:** components are composed from primitives.
  - **Shared fixtures:** the gallery and the component tests use the same fixtures.
  - **One code path:** no screen is drawn any other way than through the real view component.

## Shared contract (another agent is writing the coding plan in parallel and relies on these exact names)
- Tokens: `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css`, using Tailwind 4 `@theme` variables. The light palette is defined on `:root`; dark comes from `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])`, and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, so it works both in the app and in the artifact viewer, which sets `data-theme`.
- Primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui/` (for example button, text field, checkbox, search box, task row, sortable list, empty state, inline confirm, notice or banner, skeleton). Choose the set the screens need, nothing speculative. App shell: `frontend/src/components/app-shell.tsx` (`AppShell`).
- Views: props in, JSX out. No data fetching, no TanStack Query, no router hooks inside a view; callbacks out. Files:
  - `frontend/src/views/sign-in-view.tsx` (`SignInView`)
  - `sign-up-view.tsx` (`SignUpView`)
  - `task-list-view.tsx` (`TaskListView`)
  - `task-detail-view.tsx` (`TaskDetailView`)
  - `not-found-view.tsx` (`NotFoundView`)

  Export each view's props interface. Design the props so a container can wire TanStack Query to them later without the view changing. Local UI state (a draft form value, an open confirm) may live in the view with `useState`. Server data never does.
- Every state the spec implies must be expressible through props and shown in the gallery:
  - Task list: loading, empty, error, ready with completed and open tasks and a due date, searching with results, searching with no results, reorder disabled while searching, a pending create.
  - Task detail: viewing and editing, saving, field errors, "Changed elsewhere" (newer version under an unsaved draft), the delete confirm, not found.
  - Sign in and sign up: idle, submitting, field errors, wrong credentials (401), email taken (409).
- Reordering uses dnd-kit with pointer, touch and keyboard sensors. The view emits `onMove(taskId, afterId | null)`.
- Zod schemas: `frontend/src/lib/schema/task.ts` (`taskSchema`, `Task`, `taskListSchema`) and `frontend/src/lib/schema/auth.ts` (`credentialsSchema`, `userSchema`, `User`). Fields follow spec D8 plus `id`, `rank`, `version`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, camelCase. Types come from `z.infer`. Title is 1 to 200 characters, notes at most 5,000, password 12 to 128. Forms validate with these same schemas.
- Fixtures: `frontend/src/test/fixtures.ts`, realistic task content, shared by tests and the gallery.
- Design gallery: a second Vite entry at `frontend/design/` (`index.html` and `main.tsx`). It renders a token sheet (colour swatches with names and contrast ratios, the type scale, spacing, radii, motion) and then every view in every state, each at phone width (390 px) and desktop width (1280 px) frames. `npm run design:build` produces one self-contained HTML file at `frontend/design/dist/artifact.html`:
  - **Inlined:** all JS, CSS and fonts. Self-host fonts with `@fontsource` packages, so the app and the gallery share them, and inline them in the design build only.
  - **No wrapper tags:** no `<!doctype>`, `<html>`, `<head>` or `<body>`. The artifact host wraps the file itself, so strip them in a small post-build step, and put a `<title>` near the top.
  - **No network calls,** and nothing relying on browser storage.
  - **Under 16 MB.**

## Frontend scaffold (yours to create, since the views need it)
- **Toolchain:** Node 24 and npm (commit `package-lock.json`), Vite, React 19, TypeScript strict (also `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`), Tailwind 4 via `@tailwindcss/vite`.
- **ESLint** (flat config):
  - `typescript-eslint` strict and type-checked rule sets.
  - `react-hooks` with `rules-of-hooks` and `exhaustive-deps` as errors.
  - `no-console` as an error, allowing only info, warn and error.
- **Prettier.**
- **Testing:** Vitest with jsdom, React Testing Library, user-event and jest-dom. The coverage threshold is 85% lines and branches in `vitest.config.ts`.
- **Scripts:** `dev`, `build`, `check` (ESLint + `prettier --check` + `tsc --noEmit`), `test` (Vitest with coverage), `design:build`.
- **`frontend/CLAUDE.md`:** short, covering commands, layout and gotchas. The root `CLAUDE.md` already points to it.
- **CI:** add a `frontend` job to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (npm ci, check, test, build).
Don't add the router, TanStack Query, MSW or a fetch wrapper; those come with the data layer later.

## Engineering rules that bind you
- **Test first:** red, then green, inside your session. Every commit is green: `npm run check && npm run test && npm run build` all pass before each commit.
  - Test behaviour a user can see: roles, names, text, callbacks fired with the right arguments. Never test class names.
  - Each view gets tests for its states, and interactive primitives get tests for their interactions.
  - No redundant tests: a primitive's behaviour is tested once on the primitive, not again through every view.
- **Functional, declarative style:** pure helpers (for example date formatting, due-date status) are exported and unit-tested, with no mutation (use `toSorted` and friends).
- **JSDoc** on every export. Kebab-case files. Named exports. Accessible markup: labels, real buttons, visible focus, 44 px touch targets, responsive from 320 px.
- **Visual QA is mandatory:**
  - Use Playwright (as a dev dependency; run `npx playwright install chromium`) to screenshot the built gallery at 390 px and 1280 px wide, in both light and dark (set `data-theme`).
  - Look at the screenshots with your Read tool and fix what you see: alignment, contrast, spacing rhythm, overflow, anything that isn't premium.
  - Save the final screenshots under `frontend/design/screenshots/` and commit them, so the lead can see them in the PR.

## Constraints
- Work in your worktree. First create and switch to branch `feature/web-design-system`.
- Touch only `frontend/`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the frontend job) and nothing else. Never read or write `.env` files.
- Conventional commits (`feat(web): ...`, `chore(web): ...`, `test(web): ...`) with why-focused bodies, one logical change each, each ending with the trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Do not push and do not open a PR.

## Work in two phases. Stop after phase 1.
**Phase 1, the direction checkpoint:**
1. The scaffold.
2. The tokens, with a short written rationale: the vintage source, the palette with names and roles, the type pairing, the spacing and radius scale.
3. The primitives that `TaskListView` needs.
4. `TaskListView` in all its states.
5. The gallery showing the token sheet plus `TaskListView`.
6. Screenshots at both widths and in both themes.

All committed and green. Then STOP and end your turn with the phase 1 report below. The tech lead will review the direction and either send corrections or tell you to continue.

**Phase 2, only after the go-ahead:**
1. The remaining views with all their states, plus `AppShell`.
2. The full gallery and the final screenshots.
3. `frontend/CLAUDE.md` and the CI job.
4. A final self-review against this brief.

## Report format (end of each phase)
- **Branch and commits:** the branch name and the commit shas with their subjects.
- **Tests:** the exact pass counts and coverage numbers from your last `npm run test`.
- **Direction:** the design direction in 5 lines (source, palette, type, feel).
- **Screenshots:** their paths.
- **Decisions:** any you made that the brief didn't settle, with reasons.
- **Weaknesses:** anything you're unhappy with, or would do with more time.

You are the planning engineer on `todo-app`, a full-stack To Do list built for an engineering challenge that will be reviewed line by line in a live deep-dive. Your job: write the detailed coding plan for round 1 (the app running in containers). You write a plan document, not code.

## Read first, in full
- `TASK.md` (the challenge brief), `docs/kickoff.md` (requirements, the lead's feedback verbatim, locked decisions), `CLAUDE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, every file in `.claude/rules/`.
- `docs/specs/round-1.html`: the signed-off spec, decisions D1 to D20. It is the source of truth. Read the HTML text closely, including the tables and the figure captions.
- `FUTURE.md` (what is out of scope).

## Goal
Produce `docs/plans/round-1.md`: a plan precise enough that an engineer could build round 1 from it without making a design decision the spec didn't already make, and that the lead can skim in tables. Every spec decision (D1 to D20) must be traceable to where the plan implements it.

## Scope: what the plan must contain
1. **Traceability table:** spec id to plan section(s).
2. **Repo layout:** every backend module and file with one line on what it owns (functional core in `backend/app/domain/`, thin routers, services, repositories, db models, settings, app factory, middleware). Frontend data layer and containers (see the shared contract below). `e2e/` (live API tests, Playwright), `load/` (k6), compose and Docker files.
3. **Backend detail:**
   - Settings: every env var, its type, default, and whether it's required. Then the exact lines for `.env.example`. The human creates that file; agents never write it.
   - App factory, lifespan (pool create and dispose), middleware (request id, access log, `X-Served-By`, `Origin` check on writes giving 403), exception handlers (422 to 400, domain errors, one error envelope).
   - SQLAlchemy models. The first alembic migration as a DDL outline: extensions `citext` and `pg_trgm`, tables, `rank text COLLATE "C"`, `version`, checks, unique `(owner_id, rank)`, trigram GIN index, unique email.
   - Pydantic request and response models: camelCase on the wire via `alias_generator=to_camel`.
   - Domain core function signatures with their contracts. `rank_between` gets its algorithm spelled out (base-62 midpoint keys; show the worked example `rank_between("a0","a1") == "a0V"` and `rank_between("a0","a0V") == "a0F"`). Also `search_pattern`, which escapes `%`, `_` and `\`, and `apply_patch`.
   - Repositories and services, with transaction boundaries and the advisory lock placement (D16). The conditional `UPDATE` with version (D17).
   - Auth: JWT claims, lifetime and cookie attributes. argon2id with OWASP parameters behind `to_thread` and `Semaphore(4)` (D14).
   - Concurrency config: uvicorn flags (D13), pool and timeouts (D15). `/livez` and `/readyz` (D19). JSON logging through `QueueHandler` (D11).
4. **Frontend data layer:**
   - The fetch wrapper and `ApiError`, and the query key factory.
   - Query and mutation hooks: optimistic toggle, reorder and delete with rollback; reorder mutations share one `scope`; `cancelQueries` before optimistic writes; `AbortSignal` for search; 250 ms debounce.
   - `refetchOnWindowFocus`, and the "Changed elsewhere" detection for D17: a cached version newer than the draft's base version.
   - Global 401 handling, the auth context and route guard, router config, the error boundary, and `console.info`/`console.error` usage.
   - One container per route that wires a view to these hooks.
5. **Containers (round 1):**
   - Backend Dockerfile: multi-stage with uv, non-root.
   - Frontend Dockerfile: build stage, then an unprivileged nginx.
   - `nginx.conf`: SPA fallback, `/api/` proxied to an upstream with keepalive, 64 KB body limit, security headers including a CSP, probes not routed.
   - `docker-compose.yml`: `db`, a one-shot `migrate` that must succeed before `api` starts, `api` with 2 replicas, `web` on 8080 as the only published port, and a `k6` service under a `load` profile. Healthchecks for each.
6. **Test plan:** for each of the five layers plus load, list the test files and the test names (behaviour-named).
   - Every race in the spec's race table gets a named test. Say how it fires concurrent requests (`asyncio.TaskGroup`, separate connections) and how we show it fails without its guard.
   - The asyncio debug-mode slow-callback fixture.
   - Database fixture strategy: the race tests need real commits across connections, so say how test isolation works, for example a dedicated test database with truncation between tests.
   - Hypothesis properties for `rank_between`, and the Postgres-vs-Python sort agreement test.
   - The k6 script outline, its budgets, and the stepped capacity run (D18).
   - Coverage configuration (90/85).
7. **CI:** the jobs and their steps (hygiene plus hook tests exist already; add backend with a Postgres service container, frontend, and e2e with compose).
8. **Delivery sequence:** the PRs in order and, inside each, the commit sequence in test-first order: which test goes red, then what makes it green. Every commit must be green.
   - Mark the checkpoints where the lead must be present: the race tests (watch them fail without the guard, then pass) and the load test (review scripts and budgets first, then walk through the results).
   - Mark the review gates.
   - Per PR, give the size as bounded work (files, migrations, PR rounds), never human hours or days (see the workspace's time-estimation rule). Name external waits separately.
9. **Risks and open questions.** Anything the spec doesn't settle goes here as a question with your recommendation. Never decide silently.

## Shared contract with the design engineer (working in parallel on the frontend views)
Another agent is building the design system and every screen as **presentational views** on branch `feature/web-design-system`. Plan around these names exactly:
- Tokens: `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css` (Tailwind 4 `@theme`).
- Primitives: `frontend/src/components/ui/`. App shell: `frontend/src/components/app-shell.tsx` (`AppShell`).
- Views, props in and JSX out, no fetching and no TanStack Query inside: `frontend/src/views/sign-in-view.tsx` (`SignInView`), `sign-up-view.tsx` (`SignUpView`), `task-list-view.tsx` (`TaskListView`), `task-detail-view.tsx` (`TaskDetailView`), `not-found-view.tsx` (`NotFoundView`). The design engineer defines their prop interfaces.   - **No `TaskGroup` in app code.** No request has independent awaits to run together; it drives the race tests.
  
  **Open questions, with my recommendation**
  - Q-1: Move body is `afterId`, not the spec's `after_id`. Fix the spec text.
  - Q-2: Keep `--limit-concurrency 200`. The fetch wrapper turns any 502, 503 or 504 without the envelope into `service_unavailable`. Correct the spec's wording.
  - Q-3: Allow writes with no `Origin` header; reject a mismatch or `null`. Browsers always send it on writes, so its absence means a script.
  - Q-4: Services open their own transaction (`session.begin()`). Sign-in then never holds a database connection while it waits to hash, and the lock sits visibly first. Update `python.md` in PR C.
  - Q-5: Add a `test-db` compose service under a `test` profile, on `127.0.0.1:55432`, off by default.
  - Q-6: `.env.example` holds working local-only values, so a clean Mac needs only `cp .env.example .env`.
  - Q-7: Split the backend PR into `api-foundation` (C1 to C8) and `api-tasks` (C9 to C14), for line-by-line review.
  - Q-8: Keep the spec's name `apply_patch`, with a patch-to-changes contract (or rename it `changes_from_patch`).

  - Q-10: Playwright lives in `e2e/browser/`. Update `map.json` in PR E.
  - Q-11: "Review" shows the newer values beside the draft, with "Use theirs" and "Keep mine".
  - Q-12: A crash view for the route error boundary. I asked the designer for a small `ErrorView`; the fallback is `NotFoundView` with different text.
  - Q-13: Give `/api/docs` its own CSP in nginx for Swagger UI's CDN files.
  
  **Spec or rule contradictions**
  1. The spec writes the move body as `after_id`; `api-contract.md` and kickoff § 5a lock camelCase on the wire.
  2. The spec promises an enveloped 503 past the limit. uvicorn's `--limit-concurrency` reply is plain text, which I confirmed in its `flow_control.py`.
  3. `python.md` puts the transaction in a dependency. FastAPI's default `scope="request"` runs that exit code after the response is sent (FastAPI 0.118 and later; `scope="function"` arrived in 0.121), and sign-in shouldn't hold a connection while hashing.

  5. `map.json` expects `frontend/playwright.config.ts`; the brief puts Playwright in `e2e/`.
  6. `typescript.md` says "no classes", which rules out an `Error` subclass.
  7. `backend/CLAUDE.md` and `frontend/CLAUDE.md` are referenced but don't exist yet; PR C and PR D create them.

  - The Zod schemas should trim the title and use 12 to 128 character passwords.

179	### 3.3 Middleware and the Origin guard
180	
181	**`RequestContextMiddleware`**, a pure ASGI middleware. A pure one, not `BaseHTTPMiddleware`, so it runs in the request's own task and context variables flow both ways ([Starlette: pure ASGI middleware](https://www.starlette.io/middleware/#pure-asgi-middleware)). For each HTTP request it:
182	
183	1. Takes `X-Request-ID` from the request when it matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, and otherwise makes one (`uuid4().hex`). It sets the `request_id` context variable.
184	2. Wraps `send` so that `http.response.start` gets `X-Request-ID`, `X-Served-By: <socket.gethostname()>` and, for `/api/` paths, `Cache-Control: no-store`.
185	3. Times the request with `time.perf_counter()`. After the app returns, or raises, it logs one access line on logger `app.access`: `method`, `route` (the route template from `scope["route"].path`, or the raw path when nothing matched), `status`, `duration_ms`, plus `request_id` and `user_id` from the context. A successful `/livez` or `/readyz` is not logged, because probes every 5 s would drown the useful lines. A failed probe is logged.
186	4. On an exception escaping the app, it logs the access line with status 500 and re-raises. Starlette's outer `ServerErrorMiddleware` then calls the 500 handler (§ 3.4).
187	
188	`user_id` reaches the access line because `get_current_user` (an async dependency, so it runs in the same task) sets the `user_id` context variable. An integration test pins this (§ 6.3).
189	
190	**Origin guard**, `require_trusted_origin`. A dependency on `api_router`, so it covers every `/api/v1` route and raises a domain error that the handlers turn into the envelope (handlers never build bodies by hand).
191	
192	| Method | `Origin` header | Result |
193	|---|---|---|
194	| `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` | any | pass |
195	| `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` | equals `APP_ORIGIN` | pass |
196	| same | present and different, including the literal `null` | `ForbiddenOrigin` → 403 `forbidden_origin` |
197	| same | absent | pass **(Q-3)** |
198	
199	Browsers always attach `Origin` to a non-GET request, and send `null` rather than leaving it out when a policy hides it ([Fetch: append a request Origin header](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#append-a-request-origin-header)). So a missing header means a non-browser client (curl, k6, a reviewer's script), which cannot ride the user's cookie in a CSRF attack. Router-level dependencies run before the body is parsed, so a cross-origin write with a bad body still gets 403.

201	### 3.4 Errors: one envelope, one map
202	
203	Wire shape (`app/api/schemas.py`):
204	
205	```python
206	class ErrorDetail(WireModel):  field: str | None; message: str
207	class ErrorBody(WireModel):    code: str; message: str; details: list[ErrorDetail] = []
208	class ErrorEnvelope(WireModel): error: ErrorBody
209	```
210	
211	Domain errors (`app/domain/errors.py`) carry no HTTP knowledge. `app/api/errors.py` maps them with one dict, `STATUS_BY_ERROR: Mapping[type[DomainError], tuple[int, str]]`:
212	
213	| Raised by | Domain error | Status | `code` | `message` (safe to show) |
214	|---|---|---|---|---|
215	| Request validation (FastAPI) | `RequestValidationError` | 400 | `validation_failed` | "Some fields are not valid." `details` gives one entry per field, using the last string in `loc` (the camelCase alias) |
216	| Empty `PATCH` body | `EmptyPatch` | 400 | `validation_failed` | "Send at least one field to change." |
217	| Bad `If-Match` | `InvalidPrecondition` | 400 | `invalid_if_match` | |
218	| `afterId` unknown, someone else's, or the task itself | `InvalidPosition` | 400 | `invalid_position` | One message for all three |
219	| No, bad or expired session | `NotAuthenticated` | 401 | `not_authenticated` | |
220	| Wrong email or password | `InvalidCredentials` | 401 | `invalid_credentials` | One message for unknown email and wrong password |
221	| Origin mismatch | `ForbiddenOrigin` | 403 | `forbidden_origin` | |
222	| Task missing or not yours | `TaskNotFound` | 404 | `not_found` | |
223	| No route (Starlette `HTTPException` 404 or 405) | n/a | 404 or 405 | `not_found`, `method_not_allowed` | |
224	| Email registered | `EmailTaken` | 409 | `email_taken` | `details` names `email` |
225	| Version mismatch | `VersionMismatch` | 412 | `version_mismatch` | |
226	| Pool wait, statement timeout, database down | `sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError`, `OperationalError`, `InterfaceError`, `ConnectionError` | 503 | `service_unavailable` | WARNING with `where=`, `why=`, `then=503` |
227	| Anything else | `Exception` | 500 | `internal_error` | ERROR with the traceback |
228	
229	Handlers: `RequestValidationError` → 400 (logged at WARNING with the field names, never the values). `DomainError` → the map. `StarletteHTTPException` → the envelope. The database errors → 503. `Exception` → 500. A unit test walks every `DomainError` subclass and asserts it has an entry in the map.
230	
231	Two 503s cannot carry the envelope: uvicorn's own `--limit-concurrency` reply (plain text `Service Unavailable`, [uvicorn `flow_control.py`](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/master/uvicorn/protocols/http/flow_control.py)), and nginx's 502 and 504. The frontend's fetch wrapper turns any non-envelope 502, 503 or 504 into `ApiError` with code `service_unavailable` (§ 4.2) **(Q-2)**.

316	### 3.7 Domain core (`app/domain/`, pure, no I/O)
317	
318	#### 3.7.1 `rank_between`
319	
320	```python
321	DIGITS = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"  # base 62, in byte order
322	def rank_between(lower: str | None, upper: str | None) -> str: ...
323	def validate_rank(rank: str) -> str: ...  # returns rank or raises InvalidRank
324	```
325	
326	**Contract.** For valid keys with `lower < upper` (byte order, which is Python `str` order for ASCII and Postgres `COLLATE "C"` order), the result is a valid key with `lower < result < upper`. `None` means open-ended on that side. `rank_between(None, None) == "a0"`. It raises `InvalidRankOrder` when `lower >= upper`, and `InvalidRank` for a malformed key. It never mutates and never touches I/O.
327	
328	**Key format.** It follows David Greenspan's fractional indexing ([article](https://observablehq.com/@dgreensp/implementing-fractional-indexing), [reference code](https://github.com/rocicorp/fractional-indexing)). A key is an *integer part* followed by an optional *fraction*.
329	
330	- The integer part is a head letter plus digits. Heads `a` to `z` mean 1 to 26 digits (`a0`, `a1`, … `az`, then `b00`). Heads `Z` down to `A` mean 1 to 26 digits below zero (`Zz` sorts just before `a0`).
331	- The fraction is base-62 digits that never end in `0`.
332	- So appending and prepending step the integer part and keep keys short (`a0`, `Zz`, `Zy`, …). Only inserts between two neighbours grow the fraction.
333	
334	**Algorithm, as pseudo-steps.**
335	
336	```
337	midpoint(lo, hi):                  # fractions, lo < hi, hi may be None, neither ends in "0"
338	  1. If hi is not None: n = length of the common prefix of lo (padded with "0") and hi.
339	     If n > 0: return hi[:n] + midpoint(lo[n:], hi[n:])
340	  2. dlo = value(lo[0]) or 0 if lo is empty;  dhi = value(hi[0]) or 62 if hi is None
341	  3. If dhi - dlo > 1: return DIGITS[(dlo + dhi) // 2]      # floor, see the note below
342	  4. If hi has more than one digit: return hi[0]
343	  5. Return DIGITS[dlo] + midpoint(lo[1:], None)
344	
345	rank_between(lower, upper):
346	  1. Validate each key given. If both are given and lower >= upper: raise InvalidRankOrder.
347	  2. Neither given: return "a0".
348	  3. Only upper (insert at the top): (i, f) = split(upper)
349	       if i is the smallest integer ("A" + 26 zeros): return i + midpoint("", f)
350	       if f != "": return i                    # the bare integer sorts before upper
351	       return decrement(i)                     # "a0" → "Zz"
352	  4. Only lower (append): (i, f) = split(lower); j = increment(i)
353	       return j if j is not None else i + midpoint(f, None)
354	  5. Both: (il, fl) = split(lower); (iu, fu) = split(upper)
355	       if il == iu: return il + midpoint(fl, fu)
356	       j = increment(il)
357	       return j if j < upper else il + midpoint(fl, None)
358	```
359	
360	`increment` and `decrement` add or subtract one in base 62 with carry. A carry out of the head moves to the next head letter, which adds or drops a digit (`az` + 1 = `b00`, `a0` − 1 = `Zz`). They return `None` past `zzz…` or `A000…`.
361	
362	**Worked examples.**
363	
364	| Call | Path | Result |
365	|---|---|---|
366	| `rank_between(None, None)` | step 2 | `"a0"` |
367	| `rank_between("a0", "a1")` | step 5: integer parts differ; `increment("a0") = "a1"` is not `< "a1"`, so `"a0" + midpoint("", None)`, which takes step 3 with `(0 + 62) // 2 = 31` → `V` | `"a0V"` |
368	| `rank_between("a0", "a0V")` | step 5: same integer `a0`, so `"a0" + midpoint("", "V")`: no common prefix, `(0 + 31) // 2 = 15` → `F` | `"a0F"` |
369	| `rank_between(None, "a0")` | step 3: no fraction, `decrement("a0")` | `"Zz"` |
370	
371	**Note on rounding.** The reference code rounds the midpoint digit with `Math.round`, which would give `a0G` for the third row. The spec's worked example pins floor division, and any digit strictly between the two is correct, so floor it is.

383	
384	```python
385	class Unset(Enum): UNSET = auto()
386	@dataclass(frozen=True)
387	class TaskPatch:
388	    title: str | Unset = Unset.UNSET
389	    notes: str | Unset = Unset.UNSET

399	**Contract.** `apply_patch` returns only the fields that were sent, keyed by column name, built with a comprehension over `dataclasses.fields`. `due_date=None` is kept, because it means "clear".
